This research focuses on resolving inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships between attributes. Unlike conventional methods that assume the presence of unique keys, our approach accommodates tables with multiple possible keys, including those with attributes that can serve as keys in specific scenarios. Furthermore, we have enhanced the data quality framework by incorporating optional relationships between attributes, such as those where data for one attribute may be required when data for another attribute is present. We have developed a pattern-based formulation to model these situations and have established the consistency of the pattern-based model as a particular case of the standard data integration problem. Moreover, we have investigated the problem of repairing inconsistent tables and have developed a series of lower bounds on the size of the repaired tables. Additionally, we have constructed a specific repaired table for a given instance of inconsistent data and have validated that this table is optimal in terms of size. We have also explored the problem of repairing tables in a particular scenario and have developed a approach that first identifies all possible repaired tables and then selects the smallest one. Furthermore, we have a solution that is more efficient and has developed a protocol for defining specification languages that support scenario-based data repair. Furthermore, we have compared our approach to conventional methods of handling inconsistencies and functional relationships and have found that our approach is more effective in terms of size of the repaired tables. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that combines the benefits of neural networks and descriptor fields to enable efficient and robust object manipulation tasks under various environments and lighting conditions. In contrast to traditional approaches that use neural networks for object representation, NDFs utilize a single neural network to generate both object descriptors and occupancy maps in three-dimensional space. We demonstrate that NDFs are insensitive to rotation, translation, lighting, and scale through a carefully designed abstraction that employs the network's inherent learning capabilities and operational invariance. Furthermore, NDFs describe objects as collections of locally consistent points, eliminating the need for mesh-based representations and making them more resilient to category-level tasks. We showcase the effectiveness of NDFs in object categorization, segmentation, and manipulation tasks using the ModernGripper dataset and a simulated manipulation environment. The code is available at https://github.com/vishalranjan/ndf.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct tasks: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We integrated the two processes by feeding the projection map into a discriminative correspondence network, thereby establishing a unified framework capable of directly estimating object pose. Experimental evaluations conducted on multiple datasets demonstrate that the proposed architecture offers enhanced performance for difficult datasets featuring substantial occlusion. The code has been made publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ChengLi521/DeepHMap++.

Numerous biological simulations rely on detailed models of molecular configurations, yet the computational cost of determining all degrees of freedom for all molecules can be excessively high. This difficulty is particularly pronounced in various biologic systems such as cell membranes. To overcome this challenge, this work introduces a novel approach that focuses only on the relative entropy of molecule configurations. This is achieved by developing a new information-theoretic threshold that ensures the precision of configuration sampling meets the requirements of dynamical accuracy. The proposed method's efficacy is demonstrated through simulations of a model protein and a complex cell membrane, showing that it significantly reduces the computational expense while yielding precise results. The introduction of an adaptive block-size strategy further enhances performance by optimizing the information-theoretic threshold on a per-atom basis. The developed method is particularly well-suited for high-performance simulations on distributed computing platforms and can be integrated into existing molecular dynamics codes with minor modifications. The code for the proposed method is publicly available as an open-source extension to the LAMMPS molecular dynamics simulator. The proposed algorithm can also be used as a standalone tool for configuring molecules via Metropolis Acceptance Criteria. The results presented in this work indicate that the proposed method can be highly effective in biologic systems, where the spatial distribution of molecules is often nearly uniform, allowing for significant reductions in computational costs while maintaining precise precision. The potential applications of this method for forecasting complex biochemical processes, as well as for devising optimized simulation protocols, also are discussed. The results of the research have been published in the journal PLOS Computational Biology. Our research extends the concept of eigenvector centrality to multi-layer networks by taking into account the reliable calculation of node signs in separate layers. Initially, we outline a method to compute the eigenvectors of a multi-layer network using a relevant objective function that incorporates distinct centrality measures for each layer. We then establish that the significance of a node in a multi-layer setting can be determined by the prominence of its corresponding eigenvector component. To handle instances where the network lacks an intrinsic scale, we introduce a multi-layer network version of the proposed method that accounts for node signs and relies on a comparison with randomized versions of the network. Our results demonstrate that this method effectively recovers the structure and identifies central nodes across various synthetic and real-world examples. To further explore the applicability of this method, we analyze the results of a simulation where the reliability of node signs in separate layers is varied and find that the method's performance remains robust. To facilitate the use of this method for large-scale network analysis, we implement the method using a computationally efficient approach and show that it can be applied to complex multi-layer networks, including those consisting of multiple overlapping layers. To this end, we also introduce a new quality measure that evaluates the consistency of node signs across different layers of a multi-layer network. Our research provides a versatile and adaptable framework for evaluating the significance of nodes in multi-layer networks and offers researchers a range of possibilities for its further development and customization. Our code is available at: https://github.com/AminEbrahimi/EigenvectorCentralityMultilayerNetworks.

However, the way surface roughness affects the seal behavior of spheres was found to be more complex than previously assumed. Quantum states known as single-photon facilitated coherent states have interesting properties, being connected to quantum entanglement and providing a means for precise measurement tools. Despite their advantages, generating these states poses a significant challenge, specifically in identifying suitable parametric conditions. In this research, we outline a feasible approach to create these states utilizing quantum-optical catalysis, facilitated by a beam splitter and a parametric amplifier, for coherent input. We devise a method to assess the quality of these states, evaluating their fidelity and reducing their generation requirements. Furthermore, we analyze the effect of cat amplifier instability and find that over Broadband Coherence Time, the fidelity remains stable, allowing repetitive generation of high-fidelity states. Our findings also demonstrate that, in addition to single-photon facilitated coherent states, the setup can successfully generate other states, such as double-photon facilitated coherent states, by adjusting the beam splitter ratio. This includes a state that can be utilized for testing lossy amplitude damping, thereby providing a means for evaluating damping-induced decoherence in various quantum systems. This includes superconducting quantum circuits, as well as other two-level systems. In this research, we introduce a novel approach to investigate damping-induced decoherence, analyzing the connection between the state preparation efficiency and fidelity, facilitated by a simple and intuitive plot known as a generative decay matrix. This plot provides an overview of the relation between the state preparation efficiency and fidelity, offering a visual representation of the conditions under which the states' fidelity remain stable in the course of time. This research was originally published in Phys. Quantum, a journal published by the Quantum Science Publishers, in QComputation section, and is associated with the paper ID PQ-D-020.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive a complex Weyl tensor in the curvature matrix formulation. By applying a coordinate transformation, we are able to express the complex self-dual electromagnetic field in terms of its components within the Newman-Penrose formalism. Consequently, we obtain the specific components of the complex Weyl tensor, which can be compared to the derived Weyl tensor using the Newman-Penrose formalism, following the complex null tetrad basis. Additionally, we demonstrate how to determine the Ricci scalar, the Ricci tensor, and the Einstein field tensor in the complex null tetrad basis. Furthermore, we identify a formally singular solution to the Einstein field equations in the complex null tetrad formulation and analyze its key characteristics. Lastly, we provide a brief overview of the key characteristics of the complex self-dual electromagnetic field and offer some useful comments on the related research literature. Moreover, we offer a concise introduction to the Weyl curvature tensor, complex self-dual electromagnetic field, and the Newman-Penrose formalism in the complex null tetrad basis, followed by a detailed mathematical derivation of the derived equations. Lastly, we conclude by analyzing the implications of the research findings.

Code-mixed language processing, which involves analyzing texts that combine two or more languages, presents a significant obstacle for traditional NLP techniques, especially for the critical task of information extraction. A multitude of factors contribute to this difficulty, including linguistic diversity, lack of standardization, and intricate naming conventions. These challenges are particularly prevalent on the internet, where code-mixed content thrives among multilingual communities on social media platforms. This issue is further clouded by the lack of a universally accepted definition for code-mixed languages, which makes it challenging to gauge the scope of the problem. Despite these complications, code-mixed NLP appears promising, with potential applications in various contexts, including but not limited to crisis management, business operations, and academic research. Nevertheless, developers and researchers encounter several obstacles in creating usable code-mixed NLP systems, including gathering large-scale datasets, establishing a standard language model, and addressing sensitive issues like user anonymity. These challenges highlight the need for a collaborative effort from various stakeholders, including experts, regulators, and individual contributors, to address these issues and develop effective code-mixed NLP systems that meet the complex needs of multilingual communities.

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. To further understand and identify potential applications for these materials, we focused on studying the fundamental base state of Ta$_2$O$_5$. However, Ta$_2$O$_5$ exhibits polymorphism, incorporating different structures such as rasenna, ferroelectric, and orthorhombic types, which can be difficult to differentiate through experimental means. Therefore, we leveraged theoretical methods to examine the material's behavior using ab-initio and Monte Carlo simulations. By controlling for oxygen content and pressure, we were able to replicate and distinguish between previous research results, as well as identify a stable ferric structure at both high temperatures and high oxygen pressures. Interestingly, we found that this ferric structure can exhibit both ferroelectric and antiferroelectric properties, depending on temperature. To demonstrate the potential of Ta$_2$O$_5$ in device fabrication, we also explored how different processing methods could yield the desired ferric structure, ending with a theoretical design for a layered Ta$_2$O$_5$ device that showcases the material's reflective properties. Despite its promising characteristics, Ta$_2$O$_5$ remains underrepresented in scientific literature, and this study aims to contribute to its deeper understanding.

Humans naturally generate rich auditory feedback while interacting with their environment, which significantly enhances the understanding of their intentions and actions.  Despite the prevalence of auditory feedback during human activity, developing robotic systems that can efficiently comprehend and interpret this feedback remains a challenge.  This issue is particularly pronounced in scenarios where robots are instructed verbally by humans while performing manipulation tasks.  Current approaches focus on teaching robots through precise, reproducible motions, but these methods fail to account for the ease of sound-based instruction, which enables more natural and expeditious learning.  To address this shortcoming, this research focuses on investigating how robot instructors can be made more proficient at interpreting the auditory feedback associated with manipulation tasks.  Specifically, this work examines how robots can be trained to accurately perceive the patterns of sounds produced by human instructors as they perform manipulation tasks, using a combination of relative dense neural networks and reinforcement learning.  Experimental results, obtained using a simulation environment, demonstrate that robots trained in this manner can effectively understand the sounds associated with human actions, even when those actions are modified.  Furthermore, this research introduces a novel assessment metric that evaluates the compatibility between human actions and the sound patterns produced by the robot, providing valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms of sound generation and offering scope for future development.  The findings presented in this paper have been validated through a range of manipulation tasks performed on a real robot, using a more simplified sound modeling approach. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Considering the ubiquity of data sparsity, this study focuses on the multi-sparse-domain cross-domain recommendation scenario, where user preferences are sparse across multiple target domains, and therefore, recommends a user to multiple items across different domains. Conic optimization has a long history, with significant advancements in recent years, particularly in solving large-scale problems efficiently. As a result, solving conic representations of specific natural conic expressions has become a challenging task, taking even longer than traditional linear or second-order cone programs. We introduce Hypatia, an open-source Julia package designed to address this issue by solving large-scale complex conic expressions directly. This package leverages Julia's type system and multiple dispatch features to provide a concise and high-performance solution to general conic optimization problems, with support for a wide range of conic forms, semidefinite matrix functions, and sparse matrices. We also include a range of advanced solver configuration options, in addition to presolving and heating rule features to enhance problem performance. To demonstrate Hypatia's capabilities, we present three applications: sparse log-sum-exp, sparse multivariate Gaussian distribution estimation, and sparse matrix exponential computation. These examples showcase Hypatia's efficiency and the package's potential as a powerful tool for solving various sparse natural conic expressions. We also provide Hypatia for MATLAB users, with a similar API, allowing easy translation of existing codes. Ultimately, Hypatia offers researchers and practitioners an accessible and high-performance solution for solving complex natural conic expressions, with the source code available on GitHub at https://github.com/JuliaOpt/Hypatia.jl.

The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality assessment to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality assurance processes, including machine learning-based methods that utilize limited training data. This study presents a novel strategy for generalizing MRI quality assessment to unfamiliar settings by leveraging a robust framework that addresses multiple factors influencing generalization, and we demonstrate its effectiveness using a publicly available MRI dataset. Specifically, we show that considering factors related to model, dataset, and application leads to a significant improvement in quality assessment performance, and further analysis reveals that dataset factors have the most substantial impact. Additionally, our research highlights the significance of rigorous validation and performance evaluation in MRI quality assessment applications. We also propose a variety of approaches to enhance generalization, including transfer learning, data augmentation, and combination of models, and present our findings on these methods. Further, we discuss the importance of quality assessment performance evaluation and generalization validation, and present numerical results to support these claims. We hope this study will serve as a valuable reference for ongoing and future MRI quality assessment projects. We also explore and discuss possible extensions to this research, including evaluation of different performance evaluation metrics and quality assessment of brain MRI data for specific analysis tasks. We make our code available to the public through the MRI-QA GitHub repository.

The Coxeter group foundation theorem, initially proven by Bouscaren and Reutenauer, essentially states that a free group is generated by the elements of a Coxeter group if and only if its characteristic subgroup, defined by the product of its odd powers, is trivial. In this paper, we generalize this result for the B-type Coxeter groups by demonstrating that there is a close relationship between the structure of these groups and certain free products involving cyclic groups. Specifically, we show that there is a connection between the group's exponential elements and its integral powers, which allows us to restate the foundation theorem in a more intrinsic manner. Furthermore, we can derive implications for the group's exponential generators, including the fact that they form a generating set equivalent to the original group, given certain conditions are met. These conditions vary depending on whether the group's diagram contains a specific subdiagram known as a Y-shape or if it is a fundamental group. The paper also explores various examples and special cases of the foundation theorem for B-type Coxeter groups. Lastly, we provide a relevant open problem that could build upon our results. The paper's general content assumes only a basic understanding of the Coxeter groups and group theory, although some more advanced topics like the Whitehead lemma and the Baer length of a group are also used. The paper's primary focus is on presenting a new perspective of the foundation theorem rather than developing an innovative proof of the theorem itself. The paper's results can be interpreted in various ways, one of which is to view the foundation theorem as a statement about the group's exponential elements forming a free group, given that it does not contain any nontrivial characteristic subgroups defined by the product of its odd powers. This perspective on the foundation theorem can be applied to the free products of the cyclic groups more broadly, not just the B-type Coxeter groups. Reconstructing cosmological parameters via the cosmological lensing effect around Type Ia Supernovae has the potential to provide a independent, accurate measurement. As the brightness of galaxies and SN is connected through gravitational lensing, this method can also offer a independent assessment of the Hubble constant. We applied a blind approach to detect lensing distortions around nearly 3000 Type Ia Supernovae from the Pantheon sample, utilizing data from 37 foreground lenses. We identified signs of lensing fluctuations in the data, and our findings correlate with the brightness of the SN as expected. Combining the effects of multiple lenses and the overall galaxy distribution, we found that lensing modified the apparent brightness of the SN by about 4 percent on average. This finding matches the predicted effect of lensing based on current understanding of the universe. It also aligns with the same level of brightness modification caused by feeble scattering within the SN environment itself. Therefore, we interpreted the observed shift as primarily caused by lensing rather than scattering. Ultimately, we calculated the average lensing modification per SN and compared it to the predicted effect, finding that the two values are consistent. We then calculated the cosmological parameters based on the assumed standard model of the universe, and our calculations showed that these parameters match the expected values, indicating that this novel approach is both reliable and precise. This paper introduces a novel theory explaining how context affects the recall of abstract objects in deep neural networks used for recognition tasks. Our context theory consists of two parts: the first portion describes how context functions to filter out irrelevant objects by identifying objects that share the same attribute as the network's target, while the second portion explains how context influences the network to prefer currently relevant objects by arranging them in a hierarchy of importance. To support our theoretical context model, we designed a suite of experiments incorporating multiple scenarios such as contextual relationships defined by spatial configurations, semantic connections, and associations based on object attributes. Our analysis shows that our context theory accurately predicts the network's behavior in these scenarios. To further validate our model, we developed a training method that incorporates a hierarchical learning hase to demonstrate that our context theory is effective in guiding the network to learn context automatically. Our findings have significant implications for understanding context in NLP, given the analogy we draw between the network's recognition of abstract objects and the recognition of entities in NLP. Our work also introduces a novel concept of contextual recall that can be used to assess the effectiveness of NLP models in capturing the context of complex expressions. These inequalities can be applied to obtain concentration bounds for a range of functions involving certain classes of random matrices, including the inverse of a random Gaussian matrix, random Toeplitz matrices, and certain spiked random matrix models. This newly defined symplectic manifold is equivalent to $M$ by means of a homeomorphism that complements $\phi$ and is compatible with the surface structure, and it possesses the same Alteration type as $f$. The recent introduction of incompatible kidney transplants from living donors has posed significant challenges to implantation strategies. While multiple incompatible grafts can be simultaneously implanted in the recipient, the optimal method of placement remains uncertain. Recent studies suggest that, in certain cases, positioning two incompatible kidneys with different implantation sites can lead to superior outcomes, with enhanced graft survival and better patient results. This article examines current evidence on the acceptance of deceased donor kidneys with multiple-compatibility issues and presents a case where two incompatible kidneys were accepted from the same donor. We also discuss potential guidelines for accepting deceased donor kidneys with multiple-compatibility issues and discuss possible future research to be conducted. The primary focus of this article is to provide insights that transplant surgeons and medical professionals can utilize in their daily work. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word representations learned through the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Corpus, a widely used dataset for measuring the emotional content of company names and tickers. We demonstrate that the negative sentiment scores for company names and tickers essentially reflect the opposite of their corresponding positive sentiment scores. Furthermore, we find that the word representations learned via the BERT baseline system, as well as the learned embeddings via the word2vec and GloVe baseline systems, conform to a key mathematical principle that reflects the opposing nature of negative and positive sentiments. Nonetheless, we observe that the cosine similarity of the word representations learned via the BERT baseline system, as well as the word2vec and GloVe baseline systems, does not adhere to this principle. Consequently, we propose a straightforward yet effective modification to the learning objective of BERT, ensuring its word representations comply with this principle. We also propose a novel quantitative metric that can be used to assess the quality of word representations learned by different baseline systems via the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Corpus. This metric enables us to compare the effectiveness of different learning baseline systems, including static embedding systems like word2vec and GloVe, as well as dynamic embedding systems like BERT. We further develop a statistical model that can be used to analyze the word representations learned via the BERT baseline system via a general EM algorithm. We find that the learned latent variables, which represent the positive/negative sentiment of company names and tickers, conform to the desired mathematical principle. We also discover that the majority of the remaining variance in the sentiment scores remains unexplained by the proposed statistical model. We propose a straightforward modification to improve the model's explanatory power. We further investigate the influence of different contextual mechanisms on the quality of the word representations learned via the BERT baseline system and demonstrate that the peep mechanism yields the highest explanatory power. We also develop a pure supervised learning approach that enables us to directly compare the effectiveness of different baseline systems via the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Corpus. We find that the BERT baseline system yields the highest performance on this task. We conclude by suggesting that the proposed quantitative metric can be used as an ongoing evaluation platform for the word representations learned via the BERT baseline system and other baseline systems. This article presents SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM schemes that mimic the benefit of our previously proposed Wideband Waveforming technique, which combines power and bandwidth efficiently to maximize energy efficiency while meeting data rate requirements. Specifically, these new techniques leverage the availability of multiple antennas and broadbands to enhance an baseband signal meeting the rate and power constraints, thus leading to an more energy-efficient and higher data-rate than the optimal single-antenna and single-band solution. By utilizing these new equivalents, we obtained additional insights into the optimal energy-efficient data transmission strategies using multiple antennas and broadbands. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that using multiple antennas and broadbands yields an energy-efficient benefit, which can be accurately measured, in addition to the previously established bandwidth and carrie-efficient benefits. In the case of WBE with a rate constraint, when comparing the SISO-OFDM equivalent to the optimal single-carrier solution, we found that the former solution is 50% more energy-efficient when the SNR is low, while for the case of WBE with a power constraint, when comparing the SISO-OFDM equivalent to the optimal single-band solution, we found that the former solution is 33% more bandwidth-efficient when the SNR is low. Similarly, when comparing the MISO-OFDM equivalent to the optimal single-carrier solution in the case of WBE with a rate constraint, we found that the former solution is 100% more energy-efficient when the SNR is low, while for the case of WBE with a power constraint, when comparing the MISO-OFDM equivalent to the optimal single-band solution, we found that the former solution is 66% more bandwidth-efficient when the SNR is low. Finally, our results can be applied to various transmission scenarios, including backhauling, relay transmission, and device-to-device communication. In multiagent competitions, we seek a rationalizable equilibrium that is resistant to attacks or deceitful play. However, identifying a strategy profile that is both an equilibrium and collectively rational for all players is challenging, as it requires analyzing each player's private thought process. To overcome this difficulty, we introduce an efficient algorithm that determines whether a specified strategy profile is a Nash equilibrium in polynomial time, following a natural line of research initiated by Naor and Naor's result. Furthermore, we devise a new algorithm to assess rationalizability of a given strategy profile for some players in a general multiplayer setting, with a computational complexity that scales exponentially with the number of players. Additionally, we provide a concise representation of a rationalizable equilibrium in multiagent competitions, demonstrating that this representation is computationally efficient to determine. Moreover, we establish that a strategy profile is a rationalizable Nash equilibrium in a multiagent competition if and only if it is r-rationalizable. And finally, we show that a specific two-player game has a rationalizable Nash equilibrium, which can be computationally verified, even though this equilibrium is resistant to various attack techniques. This involves executing a specific sequence of attacks against a particular representation of the game's r-rationalizable equilibrium. This result extends and improves upon an earlier result by Feige and Fleischer. This research was presented at the 2020 Conference of the Game Theory Society.

An epidemic spread can lead a network to deteriorate, possibly even collapsing under the weight of infections, a phenomenon that can be avoided through the introduction of a degree of tolerance within the network model. Researchers have successfully demystified the underlying mechanics of a simple epidemic spread on a network that adapts in response to the identification of infected nodes. However, the mechanisms governing a more complex epidemic model, where the transmission of a pathogen to another node is influenced by various factors including the degree of connection between nodes and the presence of an infected neighbor, remain poorly understood. The present study seeks to explore and explain these mechanics in a desktop carrier transmission model, a mathematical framework that incorporates tolerance within network model dynamics. By analyzing a desktop carrier transmission model, we uncover the underlying critical point that determines the model's stability in response to increased connectivity. Additionally, we determine the exact ratio of the critical point to unity, providing insight into the dynamics of the model and demonstrating that the desktop carrier transmission model is equivalent to a well-known model of self-organized criticality. Furthermore, we identify a key parameter that influences the model's stability and determine the precise value of this parameter, a value that can be achieved through various means. The present study also investigates the effects of increased connectivity on the distribution of node degrees and confirms that the desktop carrier transmission model exhibits a power law distribution in this regard. The research further takes a broader perspective, applying the desktop carrier transmission model to a geographical area rather than a network, and demonstrating that the resulting model can be interpreted through the lens of percolation theory. The study concludes by providing a theoretical framework of the desktop carrier transmission model, a framework that yields comparable outcomes but through self-organization rather than the influence of a critical node distance. To improve policy enhancement using replay data, a proposed method in this study exploits a derivative of the variance of cumulative advantages to create a more targeted and efficient sampling policy, thereby optimizing the variance of return predictions. It is mathematically proven that using this method results in a lower estimate of the target policy's variance compared to traditional experience replay. In addition, it is shown that under certain conditions, the proposed approach can lead to significant improvements in policy enhancement, as it reduces the exploration-exploitation trade-off. In order to validate the proposed method, the study conducts policy enhancement using both value-based and policy-based methods and compares the results to existing approaches, demonstrating the proposed method's effectiveness in a variety of scenarios. In one case, it is found that the proposed method can achieve a target policy's performance with approximately half the amount of data typically required, showing the method's potential to be a high-efficient policy enhancement technique. In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions. Our approach to this problem combines 
multiple text generation models through a multi-objective optimization framework 
known as Text Generation in Conversations, providing a novel perspective on 
conversational text generation grounded in self-interest. Throughout our studies, 
we examined various conversational dialogue topics using text features obtained 
from pre-trained models, offering a versatile research platform for the 
community. Our data, tools, and source code are openly accessible at: https://github.com/google-research/multitalk.

A key process in mathematical physics, the 2D random log-gas model, describes the behavior of $N$ particles scattered on the circle under the influence of a random potential, and is equivalent to a system of $N$ Schrödinger operators in a random matrix setting. As $N$ increases, the statistics of these projections converge to a random hermitian matrix model, whose eigenvalues behave like the Gaussian free field on the disk. A related boundary value problem is formed by tracing the edges of a growing domain filled with the log-gas, resulting in a collection of growing random interfaces. We have investigated the properties of these interfaces as $N$ increases and have found that they converge to multiple growing Stochastic Loewner Evolutions (SLEs) driven by the Gaussian free field on the unit disk, in a specific parameter regime. We have also established that in another regime, these interfaces converge to a single SLE driven by a different type of random process, specifically the space-filling Duarte variant of SLE, and have characterized the statistics of this process. Furthermore, we have established that both of these SLEs are radial, and that the associated Gaussian free fields are conformally invariant. Our findings are consistent with the physical predictions proposed by 't Hooft and Jevicka, and can be viewed as an outcome of the SLE Gaussian free field coupling building block, being applicable to more complex situations. Our results also have implications for the physical properties of random systems at the transition point, and provide a mathematical framework for the analysis of these systems via statistical field theory. Our approach to proving these results involves developing a number of tools from random matrix theory, as well as a result on the asymptotic behavior of a specific multiple SLE valley intersection process. We investigate the neutrino dark matter scenario, considering ultralight dark matter with a mass breaking Lorentz symmetry. This assumption leads to a term that violates lepton number and contributes to the neutrino mass matrix, specifically affecting the lightest mass eigenstate. As a result, a certain type of neutrino decay becomes possible, and we calculate its rate. Understanding the meaning of conversations involves managing different semantic variations, including scope, quantification, and negation, which can result in distinct meanings, as demonstrated by natural language inference relations. In this research, we introduce a novel task and a corresponding dataset to examine the mental variety that speakers and listeners experience when discussing semantics. The task is to predict the degree of variety present in a conversation through a natural language inference relation, while the dataset, named Semantic Variety Detection, incorporates multiple indicators of variety, including statements with: different scopes (e.g., inclusive or exclusive), various quantification types (e.g., universal or existential), and different negation levels (e.g., partial or total). The dataset, available for free use by researchers, comprises nearly 20,000 text-based pairs that are rated by multiple participants for their variety by nine different metrics. In our approach, we utilize a mixture model to integrate the diversity of the dataset, incorporating a rich set of features that include linguistic elements, conversational context, and inferred semantic relationships. Our results show that achieving a high level of performance on this task is challenging due to the complex nature of natural language, which leads to confusions in our model predictions as it struggles to balance the intricate relationships between inference relations, conversational contexts, and semantic varieties. Nevertheless, our mix of hand-crafted and deep-learning-based features enables our model to surpass the current state-of-the-art performance on this novel task. Moreover, our analysis highlights areas that our model finds particularly difficult to master, including varieties related to scope, at what level of abstraction to represent natural language inference, and how to effectively integrate conversational context with natural language models. Which has implications for developing more sophisticated models that can better capture the complexities of natural language, conversational contexts, and semantic varieties. Massive rotating stars can experience pinching due to conservation of angular momentum, leading to larger equatorial radii than radial heights and ultimately leading to mass shedding when radii reach a critical point. Currently available models do not accurately simulate the mass shedding limits for rotating low-mass stars, especially those below 0.5 solar masses, due to limited conservation of angular momentum models and the exclusion of static masses with equatorial radii greater than 0.88 solar radii in traditional mass-radius equations. By using angular momentum conservation directly and rejecting the pinching effect of gravity at the equator, this research demonstrates that even further stretching of stellar bodies can lead to mass shedding and maps out the limits of stability and mass shedding for low-mass stars. Unlike previous theories, this model shows that low-mass stars can experience mass shedding at lower rotational velocities if they have radii further stretched than 0.88 solar radii, and this model extends the available mass-radius equations to include radii up to 0.92 solar radii. This research also explores the relationship between low to intermediate rotational velocities and mass shedding limits, and predicts that mass shedding will occur at slower velocities for stars with radii closer to solar radii. This model has implications for the detection of rotating low-mass stars or substellar bodies, as it suggests that the most rapidly rotating bodies below 0.5 solar masses with radii closer to solar radii may not be pulsating delta Scuti or gamma Doradus stars, but rather those with radii closer to 0.88 solar radii due to their higher critical velocities. This research also examines the possible formation of rotating low-mass stars or substellar bodies with retained magnetic energy and enough angular momentum to exceed mass shedding limits, which could potentially explain the broad range of radii observed in ultra-cool dwarfs. Although combining these sub-measures reduces the overall precision, the method to calculate this precision is often misunderstood, particularly when considering correlated measurements of different variables. As a result, researchers frequently overestimate the precision of their measurements. To rectify this, this paper illustrates the appropriate method for calculating the precision of combined measurements, using as examples the extraction of amplitude from experimental data in particle physics. To facilitate this process for other researchers, this paper also presents a concise summary of the key formulae used for combining measurements, including those with correlated systematic uncertainties. By properly accounting for the precision of combined measurements, researchers can ensure their predictions for physical properties are conservatively estimated, thus avoiding the overprediction of precision that might follow from misguided application of the method. The proposed method takes into account ProcArray's processing capabilities, memory access patterns, data transfer rates, and temperature effects, among other factors, to provide a precise solution to the problem of determining the ideal CPU frequency for each process. The development of HyperDegrade includes a case study involving an x86 processor and an ASIC processor, as well as experimental evaluations using industry-standard benchmarks and performance optimization tools. We are interested in discovering whether these agents can effectively work together to achieve a common goal, even when they are subjected to attacks from a hostile force. We approach this problem from an optimization perspective, seeking the most efficient strategy for the agents to follow in order to maximize their overall success rate despite the presence of attacks. We have mathematically proven that the most optimal strategy for the agents can be found by resolving a complex optimization problem, although in practice this is challenging due to the large scale and dynamic nature of the system. As a result, we have developed a simplified, scalable algorithm to serve as a viable alternative. We have thoroughly tested this algorithm across a range of scenarios and found it to be highly effective, even when the system is large and unpredictable. We have also compared it favorably to other, more straightforward collaboration methods. In the process of developing our algorithm, we have incured a significant computational cost, which could potentially be mitigated through advances in technology. In this work, we introduce a novel attack strategy known as Pragmatic Privacy Assaults in Vertical Federated Learning. Our method exploits users with different data attributes acting cooperatively in FL, either by sharing private messages or keeping their information private. The goal of this approach is to deduce sensitive information from users whose data are not directly accessible to the server, without necessity for initial knowledge of the target data. We establish guidelines for determining the most effective attack strategies given different user data characteristics and demonstrate how our method can successfully reveal secretive data attributes across several scenarios. Moreover, we show that our attack is credible, accountable, and hazardous to the security of the FL system by successfully revealing secretive data attributes to the server in multiple scenarios, including scenarios with multiple users, robust FL, and FL with user selection mechanisms. Finally, we provide implications for generating intelligent and secure PRP attacks and propose multiple future research directions in this domain. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChengxiangTang/PRP-ATTACKS-on-VFL.

The sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors at high frequencies is hindered by quantum fluctuations causing losses in optical elements, specifically beam splitters. Overcoming this limitation holds the key to enhancing the detectors' capability to identify gravitational waves of increasingly small magnitude. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer, an innovative configuration that converts the beam splitter's decay into relative oscillations between two independent signals, thus separating the signal of interest from background noise. This novel idea has the potential to outperform existing detectors by several orders of magnitude in their high-frequency sensitivity. Although the algorithm for extracting the signal from the beam splitters' decay poses a significant computational challenge, developing this concept further could lead to a breakthrough in searching for gravitational waves at high frequencies. The sloshing Sagnac interferometer may also find applications in measuring subtle variations in effective gravitational fields and optical refractive index. The proposed scheme has been physically implemented at the University of Pennsylvania, where it has successfully demonstrated the predicted performance. The extensive data from this experiment has been analyzed and the resulting data have been compared to theoretical predictions, with the findings presented in the form of numerical tables. The development of this novel detector architecture also raises the question of its potential utilization in other optical configurations that involve the reference beam, a topic that deserves further exploration. The current data and analytical results are available upon request to potential collaborators. The discovery of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer offers a promising answer to the long-standing challenge of detecting superposed signals in beam splitter configurations, a problem that has puzzled researchers for over five decades. The development of this detector technology provides a promising route for achieving this goal, along with related objectives, by employing the beam splitter's decay to extract coherent information from its output, even when the signal is extremely faint. The resulting information can be obtained at frequencies that are indefinitely far away from the sources of background noise, an achievement that has never been previously accomplished. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $N$-gram models still excel in many situations with low resource costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $N$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for inexpensive training and resource allocation. In our experiments, this approach yielded superior results for low-data situations and parallelized model training, achieving comparable performance with standard neural models using significantly less data and 50% less training time. Moreover, this method enabled us to validate the previous research indicating neural models' superior performance over $N$-gram models. The code for our project is available at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramResidualLearning.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on predicting two overlapping faces from a single image, with some portions potentially occluded. This face-to-face alignment enables the construction of a continuous, occlusion-free three-dimensional face model by combining the predicted faces, thus ensuring robust performance even in the presence of substantial head orientations and facial obstructions. Our proposed framework, DFDN, has been successfully applied to real-world data and has outperformed existing methods in evaluation metrics. The source code is available at https://github.com/ghr2016/SADRNet. Additionally, a trained DFDN model has been utilized to preload a standard reconstruction network, resulting in the SADRNet repository, which is available at https://github.com/ghr2016/SADRNet_reconstruction. Our approach has been shown to excel in face reconstruction tasks, surpassing existing methods, and a trained model is available for public use.

In an inflationary model, a specific scenario can lead to the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs), namely when cosmological perturbations become overly compressed or distorted, exceeding a certain threshold, and these anomalies eventually settle at the right mass scale. We'll be focusing on compressed perturbations and how they relate to an $\alpha$-attractor inflationary model, examining various parameters that influence compression and the resulting PBHs, as well as comparing our findings to constraints placed on compressed perturbations and PBHs based on observational data. Combining these considerations, we determine the minimum value of the compressive threshold that must be exceeded to prevent PBH formation and the resulting implications for specific $\alpha$-attractor inflationary models. For the models studied, we also derive the mass spectrum of PBHs as a proportion of the total density. Our results indicate that: an analytical estimation that initially suggested a particular model contained an overabundance of PBHs was incorrect as it failed to account for the correct compressive perturbation slope; in fact, this model actually contains less compressed perturbations than necessary to create PBHs of that mass, whereas it does contain abnormally large perturbations at shorter lengthscales that could create smaller PBHs; and finally, by modifying the evolution of perturbations during the transition to the radiation era, it is possible to this model to now match the predicted PBH density. Additionally, we find that the minimum compressive perturbation threshold that must be exceeded to prevent PBH formation becomes more stringent as the mass of the PBHs increases, a relation that can be approximated by a specific mathematical relationship. Lastly, for the models examined, we find that the density of PBHs is directly proportional to the scalar perturbation density, a relation that can be approximated by a specific mathematical relationship. Moreover, we also determine the specific mass scales that are protected from PBH formation by decayed perturbation regions, as well as the relation between these scales and the mass range of PBHs formed from compressed perturbations. Finally, in conclusion, this research highlights an important aspect of $\alpha$-attractor inflationary models, namely the relation between compressed perturbations, PBHs, and the scalar density, a relation that must be considered in comparing these models to observational data. Researchers who utilize silicon donor spin have reached a record for coherence time and one-qubit gate accuracy. To advance further, demonstrating the ability to execute reliable two-qubit logic operations with a strong coupling between qubits, specifically through exchange interaction, is crucial. To facilitate efficient development of large-scale quantum processors, a computational model of two-electron behavior has been created by applying a complete configuration interaction approach within a multi-valley effective mass model. By utilizing this computational model, exchange interaction, correlation, and valley effects on spin coupling were investigated for pair configurations formed by donors placed near each other. The findings show that the model successfully reproduces the behavior of silicon donor spin coupling and suggests various placement and mass-related effects on the efficiency of two-qubit operations. Specifically, with a particular mass ratio, the model predicts a van Hove singularity at certain donor separation distances, which could be identified experimentally and signal a potential hazard for two-qubit operations. Therefore, it is essential to verify the accuracy of the model through comparison with actual donor spin data, possibly using combined theoretical and experimental approaches. The proposed simulation can further facilitate efficient testing and optimization of quantum gate sequences by predicting the behavior of two-qubit systems in a range of situations. The multi-valley effective mass model provides a reliable physical framework that can be applied to a wide range of silicon donor spin scenarios. The efficiency and accuracy of the computational model have been validated by comparing the results of the simulation with actual data obtained from experiments on silicon donor spin. The proposed model can be applied to a range of situations, from small-scale quantum processors with a small number of qubits to large-scale processors with many qubits, and can be used to optimize two-qubit operations in a range of placement configurations. Our investigation examined the conductance properties of a HgTe gapless quantum well within a 2D quantum hall system. Introducing point contacts made of CdTe to the HgTe layer, we studied the effects of interface roughness on conductance. When the long-wavelength interface roughness was perpendicular to the normal of the well plane, a conductance plateau emerged in the momentum-space projection. This plateau had a specific location, reflecting the behavior of Dirac particles, and a narrow width, influenced by mass disorder caused by the interface roughness. Conversely, the conductance plateau disappeared when the long-wavelength interface roughness was parallel to the well plane. Additionally, we found that the orientation of the roughness affected the momentum-space projection of the electron wave function. This was manifested as a projection of the Fermi surface onto the z-direction, resulting from the parallel roughness. This phenomenon lacked a theoretical explanation within our study. Next, we investigated the impact of the point contacts' geometry on conductance, discovering that the width of the conductance plateau remained essentially unchanged when the contacts' depth varied in comparison to the Fermi level's distance from the $\Gamma$ point. However, we found that the width of the conductance plateau increased when the contacts' depth exceeded the Fermi level's distance from the $\Gamma$ point. This was attributed to the formation of a conductance plateau in the middle of the gap, which we had not anticipated. This phenomenon lacked a theoretical explanation within our study. Furthermore, we analyzed the electron localization lengths within the point contacts, revealing that the conductance plateau's width was influenced by mass disorder caused by interface roughness. This caused a shift of the momentum-space projection of the electron wave function away from the $\Gamma$ point. This phenomenon lacked a theoretical explanation within our study. Nonetheless, we proposed several theoretical models to explain the phenomena we observed, which are relevant to a broader class of Dirac materials. These models predicted the appearance of multiple conductance plateaus in a 2D quantum hall system, as well as the localization of electrons at the points of high symmetry within the Brillouin zone. Exact computation in graphical models is typically intractable due to their massive size, although many models boast a compact structure reflecting local relationships. We introduce a novel, concise representation--called a Brief Function (BF)--that reflects the core of a model's functionality, and we demonstrate how this representation enables the exact solution of various problems in graphical models. Specifically, we use Brief Functions to precisely determine the Most Probable Explanation (MPE) and constrained optimization problems in graphical models, and we show that this results in an exponential reduction in the computational complexity required for these tasks. Furthermore, our approach facilitates the efficient deployment of distributed memory resources for these problems, and we provide a detailed examination of our method's performance in realistic scenarios. Our empirical findings indicate that our approach delivers a superior performance compared to state-of-the-art exact algorithms and provides a significant boost in memory utilization in realistic datasets. Our methodology and Brief Functions are applicable to a broad range of graphical models, and we illustrate the derivations of Brief Functions for three representative models--Tree-Structured Factors, Factorized Markov Random Fields, and Sum-Product Networks. Our code is available at https://github.com/salemdudemuyesen/BriefFunctions.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of fluids undergo shear thickening, a sudden and extreme increase in resistance that can cause fluids to turn solid-like. Despite its surprising nature, the causes and effects of shear thickening remain poorly understood, especially in highly concentrated mixtures that can represent real-world situations. In this study, we challenge a long-standing misconception that shear thickening only occurs in highly congested mixtures and take a more general approach by analyzing the relationship between shear stress and rate of change of stress. This simpler analysis reveals the specific stress at which shear thickening begins and ends, revealing that it follows a universal pattern that can be applied to various mixtures, including those that are concentrated or diluted. Furthermore, by examining the width of the shear thickening transition region, we gain insight into the conditions under which mixtures become completely solid-like. We validate our findings using a simple model that provides a clear physical explanation for these patterns, also known as power laws. This pattern remains consistent even when the mixtures change in other ways, offering a new approach to classifying the different behaviors of complex mixtures. This classification, known as the von Mises distance, differs from traditional methods that focus on the width of the shear thickening transition region or the stress at which it begins, providing a more comprehensive understanding of these transitions. An area where Web search personalization's effect on professional research has been inadequately studied is the extent to which it leads to the missed detection of pertinent information. This study's data comes from a professional's work-related search, conducted on Google without signing in, and includes both the initial search results and the same unfiltered search results after signing in. We compared the two sets of results to measure the degree of partiality in Google's algorithm and potential overlooked information in searches. The study found that Google's Web search algorithm shows a moderate level of partiality, with a range of 26% to 39% of the additional information that may go undetected in searches. The study also discovered that the amount of partiality varies depending on the result, with higher levels of partiality observed for list-based result elements and short text blocks. Moreover, the research indicates that many relevant information elements could be overlooked, with numbers ranging from 4 to 6 in a single search. The study's findings have implications for anyone conducting work-related searches on Google, suggesting they should check beyond the usual ten blue links, consider using incognito modes, and think critically about the credibility of sources, especially list-based information sources. The study's methods are suitable for replication, and its results can be applied to Google's Search Engine outside the work context. The study's findings also highlight potential limitations of relying solely on Web search for information and the importance of other information sources, such as specialized databases, academic journals, and direct communication with experts. The study's results can be extended to other search engines' versions of Web search, including Microsoft Bing, by conducting similar analyses of search result elements and comparing them with Google's results. The study's methods can also be used to examine other aspects of Web search, such as Web search's effect on misinformation, algorithmic bias, or the effectiveness of information seeking tasks. A novel approach is proposed for accurate and motion-free T2-weighted images in respiratory scanning. 4D T2-weighted images are critically necessary for pre-treatment assessment and post-treatment evaluation for cancer patients, particularly those with liver disease, abdominal tumors, or hypermutative gastrointestinal cancers. Although advanced MRI techniques like free-breathing 4D T2-weighted images can provide high-quality data, they have limitations due to prolonged acquisition times and sensitivity to respiratory motion. In contrast, turbo spin-echo techniques can reduce acquisition time but are more susceptible to motion artifacts, resulting in low-quality 4D images in patients with irregular breathing patterns. The proposed method combines multiple respiratory-phase T2-weighted images in a turbo spin-echo technique acquired in continuous scanning, automatically adjusts imaging parameters based on previous data, and employs compressed sensing to improve image quality. The method was tested on 4D images of 50 abdominal scans with irregular breathing patterns and showed significant improvements in quality scores compared to traditional techniques. The proposed method was also found to be capable of producing motion-free 4D images in just half the time required for conventional techniques while maintaining comparable image quality to reference images acquired in isolated respiratory phases. The fabric space |N| associated with a polyhedron N encompasses topological information, capturing the topological essence of N that remains invariant under reordering of its vertices. A key representation of |N| utilizes ordered triples of the vertex set, which can be mapped to the complex Δ(V3) constructed from the set V of vertices, with ordered triples being mapped to vertices in Δ(V3). This perspective allows for the exploration of embedded structures in |N|, specifically triads, which correspond to embedded triangles in Δ(V3). Since the relationship between vertices in Δ(V3) is deterministic and does not depend on the reordering of V, the underlying topological properties of |N| are reflected in these triads. The changes in Δ(V3) mirror the changes in V, such as adding or removing a vertex, which results in Δ(V3) gaining a vertex or losing one, as well as updating the ordering of vertices in triads. These changes in V give rise to the induced subcomplexes in Δ(V3), defined by the triads containing the added or removed vertex. induced by a change in V. These induced subcomplexes encode the same topological information as the original complex |N|. Therefore, the topological properties of |N| remain unchanged under reordering of its vertex set, as demonstrated by the homeomorphism between |N| and the complex obtained by taking the union of these induced subcomplexes in Δ(V3). This approach can also handle changing triangulations of a surface, such as a changing simplicial structure on a topological surface, as triads in this case correspond directly to the simplices in the surface. Thus, the information captured in |N| is specifically focused on the topological characteristics of the underlying space, ignoring the details of its geometric representation. The fabric space |N| provides a universal framework for examining embedded structures in |N|, as well as the impact of changes in the representation of |N|. The relationship between ordered triples and the complex Δ(V3) can be further generalized to include ordered k-tuples of the vertex set V, which are mapped to vertices in the complex Δ(Vk) constructed from V. The corresponding embedded structure in |N| is represented by the triads in Δ(Vk), resulting in the definition of the complex |Nk| for a given k. The homeomorphism between |Nk| and the union of the induced subcomplexes in Δ(Vk) holds true for any k.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for triangular flow, both in gold-gold and copper-copper collisions. Initial geometric characteristics were analyzed through a multiphase transport model simulations with different collision energies and particle centralities. The results showed that the anisotropic initial geometry maintains its directionality even after particle finalization. However, due to smaller system sizes in copper-copper collisions, the triangular shape breaks down into smaller fragments, potentially affecting $v_3/\epsilon_3$ values. Our findings also demonstrated $v_3/\epsilon_3$ proportionality to the anisotropic initial geometry in both collisions, and explained the observed $v_3$ differences between two systems using this anisotropic initial geometry property. Furthermore, early-life $v_3$ measurements demonstrated a connection with the anisotropic initial geometry, offering potential in extracting anisotropic properties from experimental data. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for multiple applications like dynamic obstacle detection and reconstructing animated three-dimensional environments. Nonetheless, obtaining precise and comprehensive trajectory information is challenging and often requires costly lidar sensors with high frame rates. The method employs an assessment metric that mimics the scene flow estimation task and accurately determines the noise levels in the input data, resulting in cleaned and complete trajectory information with reduced motion ambiguity. Experimental evaluations confirmed the superiority of Self-Guided Scene Flow Estimation in comparing different baseline methods in metrics like scene flow accuracy and motion density estimation. It utilizes a novel approach called Differential Policy Learning, which compares the system call requirements of a service at successive time intervals. This approach yields a differential policy indicating the changes in needed permissions. Differential policies are further integrated into a hierarchical policy framework. The results show that Timeloops achieves comparable efficiency with a manual approach while reducing the system call learning time by approximately 86%. Soccer games consist of multiple scenarios, each requiring different tactical approaches based on the number of goals scored and the remaining game time. Coaching decisions, especially in high-stakes situations, are particularly complex and heavily debated among soccer experts and coaches. To date, empirical research on coaching decisions in soccer scenarios is limited, with most studies focusing on player performance and coach-team relationships. This study fills this gap by exploring coaching decisions in soccer scenarios using a deep reinforcement learning approach. Our results show that a more aggressive strategy is preferred in tournament-style games where drawing is not an option, whereas a more conservative approach is preferred in games with extra time available. Furthermore, we find that the most frequently advised tactics involve maintaining possession of the ball and counterattacking rather than taking risks and launching direct attacks. This study's findings can be useful for soccer coaches seeking evidence-based guidance on coaching decisions or for technology developers interested in designing soccer game experience platforms. Additionally, this research demonstrates a deep reinforcement learning application involving multiple gated observations, which can be theoretically expanded to better reflect the complex nature of soccer scenarios. Seismic waveform inversion aims to create high-quality images of the Earth's internal structure by analyzing seismic data from experiments. However, achieving accurate results relies heavily on reliable computational methods and significant amounts of data, which can limit its practical application in fields like oil and gas exploration. In recent years, machine learning techniques, particularly unsupervised optimization-based methods, have become popular for seismic waveform inversion. These methods use neural networks to optimize the inversion process, leading to better results and faster convergence, even with limited data. A particular challenge in seismic waveform inversion is addressing the ray path problem, which makes it difficult to accurately model seismic wave propagation and interpret the results. Another issue is interpreting the physically complex images generated by inversion processes, which often require additional analysis to create usable models of the Earth's structure. Despite these difficulties, researchers have successfully applied seismic waveform inversion to real-world data, including 2D and 3D land and marine seismic experiments, using a range of approaches and machines, from low-cost options like NVIDIA TX2 to high-performance computers like IBM NeXtScale and IBM Power9. These successes demonstrate the potential of seismic waveform inversion in fields like oil and gas exploration, mining, and environmental studies, as well as in geological surveys and mining industry applications. In the process of solving the ray path problem and interpreting the results of inversion processes, researchers have also developed new machine learning techniques and algorithms, providing a foundation for applying seismic waveform inversion in other fields, such as medical imaging, astrophysics, and electromagnetic inversion, among others. The effectiveness of a programmable phase disk in the context of transmission electron microscopy (TEM) has been investigated by a numerical analysis of various parameters, specifically how the disk's composition, orientation, and precise structure influence its ability to correct spherical aberration in TEM images. To achieve this, the distribution of phase shift was calculated for different disk configurations using the Riesz method, with the resulting data compared to experimental data from a TEM instrument featuring a long-working-distance objective lens with known spherical aberration. Based on these findings, recommendations have been made for optimizing a programmable phase disk to enhance the quality of TEM images, with a proposed design exhibiting a 2.5 Angstrom lattice spacing that can correct spherical aberration through focal shift variation. Moreover, this approach has been shown to be applicable to annular dark-field TEM images, with the proposed design displaying a 10 unit focal shift value in TEM images. The results presented in this study can be utilized to create a non-coherent illumination system with a programmable phase disk, capable of adjusting its structure to suit various microscopy applications, including the correction of spherical aberration, the enhancement of high-resolution information in TEM images, and the improvement of contrast in TEM images through the adjustment of focal shift. This framework, known as the FAF model, posits that the cortex's lower portion identifies abstract categories, while the upper portion recognizes instances of these categories. Although widely accepted and utilized, the model has also sparked debate and alternative explanations. Conversely, the AAF component is shown to be non-essential, as the HAF component alone recovers the features of the input data. Alternatively, the HAF component can be interpreted as isolating the aspects of the input data that are essential for generating new synthetic data of the same class. By taking a more nuanced view of the FAF model, researchers uncover a concept known as animacy structure, which describes the relationship between feature patterns and how they classify and generate new data. This animacy structure exhibits a unique organization characterized by a distinct middle layer that bridges the gap between the most detailed surface features and the underlying categorical representations. This layer demonstrates a level of complexity that cannot be accounted for by simple models such as the FAF, and it shows significant variations across different object categories, with some categories exhibiting a linear structure and others that are non-linear. Interestingly, the study finds that the animacy structure of human faces is particularly linear, with a simple two-layer model sufficient for accurately classifying them. In contrast, the animacy structure of non-face objects is significantly more complex and varied, with a non-linear distribution of features across different categories. This is particularly evident when analyzing the relationships between categories and generating new data, where faces exhibit a distinct pattern of variation that is easily recoverable with a simple model, whereas non-face objects demonstrate a more complex and varied pattern of variation that cannot be accounted for by the same model. This finding highlights the unique aspects of the animacy structure exhibited by human faces and provides a framework for understanding the underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's organization that goes beyond the simple FAF model. The potential presence of bias in vector magnetic field maps, especially in areas with weak field strengths, is a significant challenge. These maps are typically generated using magnetic inversion techniques, and various models are available to achieve this goal. However, the availability of accurate, independent measurements to validate these maps and identify existing biases is uncommon, especially for solar imaging. In this study, we analyze the behavior of three popular inversion models and a phase gradient method using the Magnetic Inversion Assessment Tool, which assesses the accuracy of vector magnetic field maps across different field strengths by comparing their projections on the Lobatto surface. This analysis is done for a set of observations characterized by different plasma properties. We discovered that the BMT and GFU models overestimate the field strength across all inclination angles, while the MFU model generally produces more accurate results. Additionally, we found that the GFU model introduces a bias in the azimuthal angle, particularly in areas with strong field strengths. Finally, we propose using the Magnetic Inversion Assessment Tool in combination with detailed plasma and thermodynamic observations to thoroughly evaluate the validity of vector magnetic field maps and identify existing biases in the analysis of solar magneto-hydrodynamic waves in the photosphere. If such observations are unavailable, we recommend using the MFU model with a safety height limit of $2.5$ in the inversion process to minimize existing biases. This model yields maps with intrinsic stability and minimal bias, even in areas with the weakest field strengths. This study highlights the significance of experimenting with different inversion models and analyzing their outcomes in the context of solar physics, where accurate data is often limited. This is particularly important for reducing existing biases and improving the understanding of subtle phenomena on the Sun.
