This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel unsupervised retrieval-based method known as ReCross, which employs prior experience to modify the model's representations and bridge domain gaps.
To support efficient evaluation, we develop a benchmark consisting of five unsupervised cross-task evaluation protocols.
Our proposed method delivers superior performance in four of these scenarios and surpasses the performance of baseline models in three of them. 
ReCross also demonstrates versatility, as it can be combined with contrasting distribution learning to further enhance cross-task generalization ability. 
Our code, data, and guidelines are available at https://github.com/ASD5/Across-Task-Generalization.

Differentially private deep learning is crucial for protecting individual data privacy in large-scale machine learning models, especially when working with sensitive information. However, it significantly increases model performance and is impractical for real-world applications due to its computational complexity. In addition to scalability issues, another challenge is choosing the optimal value for the hyperparameter $\epsilon$ that balances privacy and model performance, which has no established method to date. We introduce a novel approach to efficiently determine the optimal $\epsilon$ by leveraging a simple yet effective exploration-exploitation strategy, combining a coarse-grid search to identify the preliminary epsilon range and a gap-based learning method to tune epsilon further. We demonstrate the superiority of our approach by applying it to real-world datasets in various machine learning tasks, which shows that our method achieves better results compared to existing techniques. We also explore the relationship between epsilon and model hyperparameters, presenting a novel analysis that can be utilized as a guideline for selecting the optimal epsilon range. We make our code available at https://github.com/yourgithubusername/effective_dp.

Consider a finite group G that contains a subgroup Isom(P\S{1}) where P represents a non-degenerate bilinear form defined on the vector space V, and a involution schema $\sigma$ that respects the form P. We investigate the existence of a boolean structure within G, inspired by the concept of a boolean group. Our study reveals that such a structure is achievable if the system (V,P,\sigma) meets specific requirements, effectively generalizing an earlier result by R. M. Guralnick and A. Shalev. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an arbitrary finite group incorporating an involution schema can be categorized into three groups: those with a non-trivial center, those possessing a distributive boolean structure, and those where the involutions form a subgroup equivalent to the alternating group A_n for n greater than 2. Additionally, we establish that any finite group with a 2-group structure has a boolean structure, and that this property is inheritable. Moreover, our findings include a specific condition applicable to the finite group 2-Sylow of an arbitrary finite group, stating that it either contains an invariant form or is isomorphic to the alternating group A_n for n greater than 2. Lastly, we provide an individual result regarding the finite group 2-Sylow of the symmetric group S_n for n greater than 2, revealing that its boolean structure is determined by a specific set of defining equations dependent on n.

We applied an innovative two-part model to analyze the compositions of 34,410 stars in the Milky Way disk using a vast dataset from the APOGEE-2. The mechanism-based analysis consisted of a primary process that formed elements primarily through nuclear reactions in the sun, Earth, and barion matter, and a secondary process that accounted for elements created through nuclear reactions in the core of massive stars. The model generated maps of elements formed through both processes, revealing patterns in the distribution of elements within the galaxy. Certain elements, such as carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen, demonstrated distinct patterns based on the properties of nearby open clusters and young stars, indicating they were formed in the galaxy over a short time period. In contrast, elements like silicon, magnesium, and aluminum showed patterns similar to that of the galaxy's total stellar mass, indicating they were formed in the galaxy over a longer time period. The distribution of elements formed through both processes will help clarify the formation and chemical evolution of the Milky Way galaxy. The extensive dataset also allowed for the detection of elements like neon, which were expected to be present but had not been confirmed before. The findings from this study are relevant to ongoing and future astronomical surveys, such as the SDSS-III APOGEE-2, the Gaia spectroscopic survey, the James Webb Space Telescope, and the SDSS-IV MaNgHaPiE. The detection of these elements will help astronomers better understand the formation and chemical evolution of the galaxy, specifically the mechanisms that formed elements like neon, which are fundamental to the development of life and affect the temperature and luminosity of stars. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, a country with a significant population. In addition to the health effects, the rapid dissemination of online rumors in China exacerbated challenges for the government, businesses, and individuals. To better understand the sources of these rumors, their transmission patterns, and how they influenced behavior, we collected 8,525 rumors that appeared online between January 24 and March 31, 2020, along with associated verification statuses, geographic regions, language types, posting accounts, content categories, and factual accuracy. We analyzed these data using statistical methods and machine learning techniques to determine factors associated with rumor spread and accuracy, and evaluated the effects of being exposed to rumors on citizens' behavior in the affected regions. Our primary findings reveal that older rumors tend to spread further and remain online for longer periods, while being associated with a weaker signal indicating a greater likelihood of being true. We discovered that rumors spreading quickly often take on a linear form, whereas the distribution of rumors that spread widely follows a power law. Our research also shows that the impact of rumors on behavior, as measured by compliance with pandemic guidelines, tends to decrease over time, and that the effect of exposure to rumors on behavior follows a nonlinear pattern. To further analyze these results, we used machine learning models to evaluate features associated with rumor spread and accuracy, finding that combinations of technical characteristics, content features, and semantic features influence the dissemination and factuality of rumors. We concluded that the effectiveness of mechanisms preventing the spread of online rumors can be improved by targeting specific categories, while evaluating the impact of exposure to rumors suggests that reduced enforcement during the COVID-19 outbreak allowed rumors to spread freely, with the effect of exposure to rumors on behavior varying over time. Our research provides statistical insights and machine learning insights into the sources, transmission patterns, and behavioral impacts of online rumors in China during the COVID-19 outbreak. We hope that these findings will be beneficial to researchers, the government, businesses, and individuals fighting the pandemic and the spread of online rumors. We also propose a framework for assessing the impact of exposure to online rumors on behavior in the context of the COVID-19 outbreak, along with a set of recommendations for reducing the spread of online rumors in China during the pandemic. We hope this framework and these recommendations will be useful to our readers in the immediate future. Our study delves into the workings of neural networks and loss functions to understand this concept. We begin by exploring fundamental concepts from optimization and machine learning, including the relationship between loss functions and network updates, as well as the network's objective and its connection to generalization error. We then examine the claim that changing the loss function only affects the network's output due to a change in the bias term, but not the classification behavior for new data. Our analysis shows this statement is incorrect and we provide counterexamples to illustrate this. We also consider approaches that have been proposed as modifying the loss function or output of neural networks, including data augmentation, mixture models and robust optimization, and classify them into both categories. Our study highlights the importance of distinguishing between the network's output and its underlying structure, as well as the risk of misinterpreting the effects of loss function modification, including solutions such as validating the desired behavior on new data through thorough testing. We believe that doing so can help avoid the kinds of difficulties we have identified in order to improve the performance of neural networks in various applications. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday common knowledge reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured to follow a subject-verb-object format, encompasses a variety of reasoning strategies, including causality, effectiveness, contribution, and multiple purposes, and is backed by extensive user verification processes.  We have further developed 13 unique reasoning templates to match the diverse aspects of human reasoning and have implemented a straightforward method to combine rules through weighting, allowing for seamless integration into existing models of reasoning.  Our findings, demonstrated across a range of challenging natural language generation tasks, showcase the vast potential of ATOMIC for guiding models of inference and verifying the validity of reasoning rules derived from this atlas.  This comes in the form of substantial improvements to tasks like Inference Reasoning and an intuitive explanation of unknown texts, along with a fascinating analysis of reasoning protocols exchanged between humans.  We have made ATOMIC available to the public for further exploration and utilization.

To enhance speech recognition using state-of-the-art transformers, two issues need to be addressed: incorporating external knowledge from text datasets and minimizing reliance on vast amounts of labeled audio data for training. To tackle these challenges, we propose a novel bidirectional multi-modal attention approach that allows for the exchange of information between speech and text. In the encoder, a speech-oriented focus module helps the model better understand audio data by incorporating knowledge from the text, while a text-oriented focus module in the decoder enables the model to generate more coherent text based on the audio input. We also explore a multi-task training method that combines speech recognition with hidden markov model training for an improved model. Our proposed approach achieves significant gains in speech recognition accuracy on Librispeech. Specifically, we observe a 12.5% reduction in word error rate (WER) when moving from a speech transformer to our proposed model, with further improvements in test-set WER of 4.3% absolute in the clean condition and 3.5% absolute in the noisy condition after 600k training iterations. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChenXuTian/S2T-MT.

Airborne transmission of diseases in confined spaces is a significant concern, and the level of mixing assumed in existing models can greatly impact predictions of infection spread. To address this issue, we propose a novel airborne transmission model specifically applicable to closed environments, which takes into consideration the distinct movements of individuals within a space. We demonstrate the relevance of our model to an urban bus scenario and evaluate the propagation of an illness among passengers using different seating arrangements, airflow patterns, and coughing breath radii. Our findings show that our model effectively replicates the behavior observed in previous epidemiological studies relying on a well-mixed framework, and reveals how the distribution of passengers can significantly affect the spread of a disease, as well as the basic reproduction number $R_0$. Our results also indicate that the basic reproduction number $R_0$ can serve as a useful predictor of illness spread in a bus, with values of $R_0$ greater than 1 indicating that the disease will spread, while values less than 1 indicate that the disease will decline. We further analyze the relationship between $R_0$ and various transmission control measures, presenting a graphical representation that illustrates how reducing the frequency of individuals' movements within a bus, increasing the airflow speed, and improving air ventilation systems by increasing the airflow speed or enhancing the coughing breath radius, all contribute to decreasing $R_0$ and thereby preventing the spread of a disease. We also explore a simple stochastic model of infection spread, and demonstrate how our previous findings can be applied to this model, which includes randomly occurring coughing events. Our research provides a previously unreported illustration of the basic reproduction number $R_0$ for an urban bus scenario, with values of $R_0$ ranging from 1.035 to 4.061, and emphasizes the significance of considering the distinct movements of individuals within a space, as well as the role of ventilation systems and airflow patterns, in predicting the spread of diseases in confined environments. Our model has been made available online for further investigation and testing. The underlying principles of our model can be applied to other similar transportation scenarios, with minor modifications, providing a valuable tool for epidemiologists and transportation specialists in preventing the transmission of diseases in these settings. The spin-orbit proximity effect in the (Bi/Co)3 multilayer stack is examined by calculating the spin-dependent resistance and spin pumping parameters. Calculations show that the spin-orbit proximity effect is strongest in the immediate vicinity of the interface between cobalt and bismuth, and its influence extends approximately three layers away from the interface. Notably, the increase in the spin pumping length in (Bi/Co)3 stacks occurs when the average thickness of the cobalt layers is below three times the mean free path, where boundary scattering dominates. As such, the spin-orbit proximity effect in these stacks is driven by boundary scattering, which enhances the spin pumping length and maintains the high level of the spin-orbit proximity effect. This finding is particularly relevant for the utilization of bismuth as a layer to create massive spin-orbit coupling in all-layer stacks, which can be applied in the development of advanced spin-orbit coupled materials, including 2D Weyl semimetals and all-layer heterostructures consisting of 2D materials and bulk materials. This research was conducted in collaboration with the Leeuwenhoek Research Institute for Chemistry and Technology at the University of Gdansk.

To solve the equation, the fractional Schrödinger equation is transformed into a form that can be solved using the method of separation of variables. The time-invariant part of the equation is then solved to determine the ground-state wave function for a general Mie-type potential in dimensions one, two, three, and four, and the ground-state energy in dimensions one, two, and four. The results are compared to previous work, and the impact of the fractional parameter on the ground-state energy is graphically presented in dimensions one, two, and four. We introduce a novel regularization technique that leverages the concept of Lipschitz continuity to improve neural networks. In order to maintain consistency, we impose the same level of Lipschitz character on both the individual components and the composite model, thereby enabling the creation of more stable and consistent models. The proposed method's advantages were demonstrated through comprehensive testing, and our findings show that it outperforms existing approaches in multiple scenarios. Specifically, we found that enforcing Lipschitz continuity yields superior results for a range of classification tasks, including Cifar10 and SVH, and that it successfully prevents overfitting in models trained on small datasets. Additionally, our technique can be seamlessly integrated into existing neural network frameworks with minimal modifications, and we included detailed implementation guidelines to facilitate this process. Our research into the proposed method also raised interesting theoretical questions, and we hope that our findings will inspire future advances in this area. We investigate the production of high-mass Drell-Yan pairs in a framework that includes third-generation vector leptoquarks, specifically GQW's, which couple to third-generation fermions via gauge interactions. We calculate these processes at a precise level, taking into consideration the effects of QCD, and provide numerical results for the relevant cross-sections. We also discuss the potential of Drell-Yan pair production at the LHC, particularly for the GQW systems with charge combinations of (++, --), (+-, -+) and (+, -), to identify potential peaks in cross-section values of 10 fb^-1 or greater. These cross-section values are calculated for a range of mass combinations, from 300 GeV to 1000 GeV, and demonstrate how the cross-sections scale with different mass scenarios. We further provide a tool that allows for the calculation of cross-section values for any mass combination, along with a discussion of how these cross-sections vary with different LHC energy settings. In addition, we show that the cross-sections for the GQW systems with charge combinations of (+, -) and (+-, -+) include signals for same-sign Drell-Yan pairs, which could potentially be distinguished from background processes based on the rapidity differences between the pair particles. We also explore the potential of these processes at future electron-proton colliders, which could provide even more precise cross-section calculations for same-sign Drell-Yan pair production. We believe that this investigation highlights the utility of Drell-Yan pair production processes and the ease with which they can be detected, making them suitable for use in vector leptoquark searches. We further believe that this investigation complements other search strategies for vector leptoquarks, which typically focus on processes that involve third-generation fermions, and provide numerical results for the relevant cross-sections, along with a tool that allows for the calculation of cross-section values for any mass combination, based on the NLO+PS QCD predictions. Radiation exposure and cost considerations make reducing PET scans' dose efficacy appealing, yet achieving this goal while maintaining diagnosis accuracy poses significant challenges. To address this issue, deep learning-based PET reconstruction methods have been developed to compensate for lower dose scans, but these models struggle with instances that differ significantly from the training data, such as scans with altered scan protocols or certain medical conditions. These models' performance also tends to prioritize grid-based pixel values over physiological surface information, which can be diagnostically crucial, but is difficult for them to incorporate effectively. To overcome these limitations, we've developed a robust deep learning framework that seamlessly integrates physics-based modelling of image formation, data, and output uncertainty, enabling the incorporation of essential surface information and facilitating performance that generalizes to instances that differ from the training data. This framework's performance was assessed using actual PET scan data and compared to cutting-edge deep learning baselines, and the results showed that it not only reduces dose efficacy but also reduces the frequency of Diagnosically Acceptable Dose Reduction (DADD). From 10Gb PET scans to 1.5Gb dose-reduced scans with a DADD of 88%, showing a 93.5% DADD performance of 4.5Gb reduced-scans. Additionally, it was found that enhancing the model's resilience through careful training data curation is more effective than using robust deep learning techniques. This research was applied to actual scans of patients with lung cancer and showed that a dose reduction of at least 50% is possible while maintaining a DADD of 90%, reducing dose efficacy and cost considerations while minimizing diagnostically acceptable reduction. This framework's capability to handle uncertain scan protocols and medical conditions, combined with its focus on incorporating surface information, makes it a versatile tool with numerous potential applications in medical imaging. This work has been published open-source, and the code is available at https://github.com/DeepLearningGordon/PhysicsGuidedUncertaintyAwareMM.

Furthermore, this analysis identifies regions of favorable and unfavorable filling configurations, offering a practical guideline for optimizing energy recovery linac designs. The proposed dimensionless parameter provides a universal understanding of beam disruption instability that can be applied to various applications beyond energy recovery linacs. We designed two distinct criteria to identify binary asteroids within the Pan-STARRS1 archival data using quasi-symmetrical asteroid orbits as a framework.  Criteria involving the assessment of specific orbital parameters to determine pairs with similar heliocentric distances, and a second based on the distinct velocities of the objects relative to each other, were employed to detect potential binaries.  A statistical model was developed to estimate the number of binary candidates arising from pairs sharing the same spectral type, orbital planes, and tidal characteristics.  After accounting for false positives and candidates with uncertain morphological classifications, approximately 0.4% of the detected objects are believed to be binary asteroids.  A comparable group of main belt asteroids without binary candidates was created for comparison purposes.  A customized version of the DRSTARFIELD Python library was utilized to extract and analyze data from Pan-STARRS1 images.  The results were further validated using a separate dataset of known binary asteroids observed by other telescopes.  The prevalent binary asteroid population appears to be restricted to the asteroid group known as binary near-Earth asteroids.  The proposed research methods and analytical results provide a foundation for discovering binary asteroids within larger asteroid groups using a similar approach.  The involvement of external factors such as planetary perturbations and critical tidal characteristics in binary formation remains unclear and requires additional study.  The promotion of future observations and spectroscopic classification to better understand binary formation and termination processes is also encouraged.  The availability of raw data and customized code used in this research is publicly accessible for use by fellow scientists.

We introduce the GPT-3 based model, AI Dungeon Master, which engages in conversations with players in Dungeons and Dragons tournaments. To evaluate this model's ability to follow the game's rules and understand the perspectives of its opponents, we created a theory-of-mind framework consisting of the Intentional Action Model. This model assesses the model's intentional actions by considering three aspects: the accuracy of its in-game decisions, the truthfulness of its statements, and the malicious intent it demonstrates in the game. Utilizing the Intentional Action Model, we evaluated the model's performance in six tournaments, discovering that it excels in both the accuracy and truthfulness of its actions but struggles with malicious intent. Furthermore, we found that AI Dungeon Master's ability to anticipate the opponents' perspectives correlates significantly with the complexity of the scenario. In addition to evaluating the model, we developed two variants of the theory-of-mind evaluation framework, one with adjusted standards for the assessment of intentional actions that reflect the unique requirements of Dungeons and Dragons. These variants demonstrate the versatility of the Intentional Action Model, showcasing that the model can be applied across diverse contexts beyond Dungeons and Dragons. Recent advancements in counterfactual reasoning have focused primarily on categorical data, whereas the potential for machine learning models like counterfactuals in structured and stochastic cases has remained underexploited. To address this gap, we develop a framework called DISCO, which generates phrasal counterfactual instances for any input text. To demonstrate the versatility of DISCO, we pair it with two different tasks: a classification benchmark, where counterfactual samples are used to train a model, and a fact-checking application, where counterfactuals are employed to verify the truth of statements. In both scenarios, our results show that counterfactuals generated using DISCO significantly enhance performance compared to conventional approaches. Moreover, we discover that counterfactual generation via DISCO is highly effective for addressing issues such as model bias and overfitting. We make the code and models developed during this research available at the website: https://github.com/PranavTyagiDISCO/Disco.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring data conditioning by learning an inverse mapping from conditional labels to data. Nonetheless, utilizing this trained model to make predictions for new data is challenging due to the conditioning process, which generates a transformed label in the data domain rather than a new conditional label. We propose an approach to leverage the inverse mapping by treating the generated label as a multi-label instance, where the model's ability to condition can provide valuable insight into the structure of data and labels. We demonstrate this proposal in a concrete problem, where the aim is to discover multi-label instances from single positive labels. The model conditions on the given label to generate a label that represents a data point in the label domain, thereby enabling the derivation of additional relevant labels. We evaluate this proposal on real-world datasets and compare it against existing methods by assessing the additional labels' accuracy and the impact on classification performance. The results show that using the proposed model's generated label leads to a 10-20% improvement in classification performance based on random index scores. Moreover, we discover that the model's ability to condition effectively is essential, and a 30-40% drop in performance occurs when the condition fails due to an incorrect label, demonstrates the significance of accurate labeling in machine learning tasks. We also explore the possibility that the recently discovered most energetic jets may have distinct characteristics, and find that the record holder for the most energetic jet, M87*, could be driven by a super-long accretion disk extending far beyond the black hole. According to this model, the proton temperature remains relatively low, the emission is dominated by non-thermal electrons within the first 10 parsecs from the black hole, and the massive protons reaching the farthest ends of the disk may account for the recently observed high-energy neutrinos. However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and varying recording techniques.  To address this challenge, this study proposes a novel method for heart sound categorization that incorporates two key features to enhance accuracy in noisy recordings.  Firstly, a wavelet-based frequency-based approach and a nonlinear scale-based approach using entropy are combined to categorize sounds by their frequency content.  Secondly, a new feature called spectral spread is introduced to capture the noise distribution within recordings.  To evaluate the effectiveness of this method, experiments were conducted using publicly available datasets with different levels of additive noise and real recordings from the pediatric population.  Results show that the proposed method outperforms existing techniques in terms of accuracy, even in recordings with heavy noise.  Furthermore, the proposed features are utilized to develop a nonlinear support vector machine model, which is found to be highly accurate in distinguishing normal and abnormal heart sounds.  This method has significant potential applications in evaluating cardiac abnormalities in children, particularly for healthcare professionals who rely on cardiac auscultation sounds at the pediatric level. The proliferation of wearable devices for monitoring physical and mental health enables continuous data collection, leading to potential applications in personalized medicine. However, data privacy concerns prevent the exchange of user data, making it challenging to develop accurate machine learning models. In response, federated learning has been proposed to train models on decentralized data. Yet, research is hampered by several issues, including limited data and different feature sets in various institutions. This study addresses these challenges and presents FedHealth, a federated transfer learning framework for wearable data in a university setting. Although universities often have rigid data management policies, inter-university collaborations can facilitate transfer learning, reducing the need for numerous training datasets. Furthermore, intra-university collaborations are often possible, enabling model development through fully supervised learning. Building on existing federated and transfer learning techniques, FedHealth employs scenic federated transfer learning, where the central server acts as the anchor model, and mobile devices are target models. This approach allows for the transfer of knowledge between universities with different data features, promoting successful adaptation in a university setting. To enhance model development, this study employs wearable data from a single university during the initial training phase. To accommodate universities with restricted data sharing policies, this study utilizes semi-supervised learning to enhance model performance. To accommodate different data distributions in various institutions, this study employs federated transfer learning, which reduces the need for numerous training datasets. Experimental evaluations were conducted using real-world data from wearable devices in two university settings, with different data distribution profiles. The results demonstrate the superiority of FedHealth, as well as the significance of inter-university and intra-university collaborations in wearable data analysis. The most optimal parameter configuration for FedHealth involves: (1) inter-university federated transfer learning with 5 iterations, (2) semi-supervised learning with 50% labeled data, and (3) intra-university federated transfer learning with 3 iterations. The outcomes highlight the efficacy of FedHealth in real-world settings, with potential applications in university research parks and start-ups. The framework has been made available open-source on GitHub, enabling further development and customization. The study also presents a unified dataset repository for wearable device data, potentially enriching the field of physioinformatics. The development of FedHealth has further inspired a new concept, called Federated Activity Analysis, which enables the assessment and tracking of physical and mental activities in mobile devices. We examine the potential output of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) for a specific type of leptoquark pair production - namely, pairs of different leptoquark types - with the assumption that only two leptoquark pairs exist as fundamental particles. Existing research has demonstrated that in many scenarios, only one leptoquark type would be detectable through LHC data. In contrast, our analysis highlights multiple situations in which both leptoquark types could be identified, often with distinct signature patterns, and where the LHC with its current energy level can effectively identify both pairs - with or without the aid of a 100 TeV Future Circular Collider. Our study covers various combinations of leptoquark charges and classifications, including both scalar and vector leptoquarks. Furthermore, we provide a range of predictions for possible LHC outcomes, from both the ATLAS and CMS experiments, based on existing data and potential future sensor upgrades. We have investigated the significance of external radiation field stimulation of molecular gas, specifically HCN, HCO+, and CI, in a statistical approach using data from the SEVEM C{\sc ii} map and different radiation field models. Our results show that the HCN/HCO ratio is largely unaffected by external stimulation, while the HCO+/C{\sc ii} ratio is influenced by both stimulation and gas temperature. Furthermore, we found a more substantial correlation between the HCN/HCO and HCO+/C{\sc ii} ratios than expected based on thermal equilibrium scenarios. Since external stimulation is likely greater than predicted in many galaxies, it may also impact observations in other molecular transitions, making it a potentially useful consideration for interpreting data, especially in the submillimeter range. Notably, we observed that galaxies with higher mass reservoirs exhibit both stronger stimulation and greater gas temperature, suggesting a connection with the physical properties of the galaxies. To further explore this, we divided the data into different ranges of stellar mass and gas reservoir mass, and analyzed the distributions of stimulation and gas temperature within these subsets. Our findings suggest a role for external stimulation in influencing the thermal balance within molecular gas, which could be particularly apparent under subthermal conditions. It is also possible to use the C{\sc ii} map to infer gas temperatures in areas with strong stimulation, which in turn allows for a better understanding of the molecular line ratios in these regions. Our analysis implies that the HCN/HCO ratio may be a more sensitive indicator of stimulation than the HCO+/C{\sc ii} ratio in areas with moderate stimulation, while the opposite holds true for more extreme stimulation. Finally, we found that the distributions of stimulation and gas temperature are independent of the environments in which the galaxies reside, suggesting that the relationship between stimulation, gas temperature, and line ratios is primarily determined by external factors, and may therefore be useful for interpreting observations in other galaxies. It is also possible to apply this analysis to individual sources, as we demonstrate with the example of ULIRGs. Our approach provides a framework for exploring the conditions in molecular gas reservoirs through the stimulation of molecular lines, which can be extended to other transitions and observed in other galaxies, as shown with the example of the giant star-forming molecule GMC. As the formation of these binaries is likely random, their orientations will vary greatly, leading to an asymmetrical detection rate. Specifically, PTA experiments will likely preferentially detect binaries with an elliptical shape oriented in an "egg-shaped" manner. To efficiently discover these binaries, a new method has been developed which employs an apparatus indicating the level of orientation asymmetry. This process is precise and efficiently converts spinful atoms into molecules with the same parity as the initial dimer state. Our calculations demonstrate various relevant coefficients for different initial state conditions. Furthermore, our model assumes that the binding energy of the dimer is negligible, allowing an approximation of spinless dimer states as a superposition of two photons. This leads to a key innovation - an atom-molecule interaction term that involves a large number of photons can now be accessed through this recombination channel. This previously hidden interaction effect could potentially steer quantum trajectories in trapping systems. Our findings also highlight the significance of initial state broadening, as it leads to an increase in the efficiency of recombination, as well as affecting the coefficients of laser-induced three-body recombination. Initially, this efficiency increase results from initial state broadening, but it eventually leads to a decline as the broadening becomes more significant and the efficient recombination occurs within a smaller trapping region. Our proposed hierarchical storage system (HSS) utilizes two levels of storage: a high-capacity, less-performant base storage and a more efficient, though less capacious top-tier storage. To optimize performance and expandability, the HSS organizes data across these storage types using a hierarchical structure, specifically a multi-level tree, and allocates space and processing resources for optimal output. Our research focuses on efficiently managing and updating the hierarchical data structure, particularly in responding to query requests and implementing data refresh operations. To enhance performance, we introduce a simplified hierarchical structure based on a set of predefined rules, which simplifies tree construction and accelerates query processing. Furthermore, our approach facilitates selective update options for the tree, enabling us to efficiently manage and maintain the balance between data retention and storage efficiency. We have implemented our hierarchy storage system using FPGA technology and conducted performance assessments, which demonstrate its effectiveness in real-world applications. Our findings show that our HSS outperforms a flat storage system in terms of data storage efficiency and achieves comparable performance in various benchmark tests. We have made our HSS source code available online, inviting the computational community to build upon our work. Our proposed storage system has significant potential uses, including but not limited to, secure and efficient data storage for internet of things devices, finite state machine-based applications, and hardware acceleration for machine learning. We have further developed a command-line tool for our HSS, facilitating easy access and simplifying the process of creating, loading, and deleting nodes in the hierarchical structure, as well as executing SQL query commands. We have evaluated this tool in various storage capacity scenarios and found it to be a highly effective data storage solution for various real-world applications. We have subsequently expanded our HSS design to include multiple FPGA devices, implementing a distributed storage system that accelerates data storage and retrieval operations across the FPGAs, and achieving a 20 times performance gain over a single FPGA implementation. Determining the precise factors influencing the shift in mass ratio between galactic stars and gas observed during cosmic time remains a key challenge in astronomy. A potential explanation for this ratio decline is supported by observations showing a paradox: although the assembly of massive galaxies accelerated in the early universe, their current star formation and stellar masses exhibit a decelerated growth. A current hypothesis suggests this paradoxical behavior is caused by massive galaxies' rapid bulge construction during the universe's infancy. We propose that the construction of bulges during this period would also account for the turn-over in the mass ratio between stars and gas observed in the mass function of galaxies. Combining comprehensive galaxy datasets from various observations, we analyzed the relationship between bulge construction and the mass ratio turn-over, and confirmed its validity. Furthermore, modeling the evolution of galaxies based on these findings, we showed that a bulge construction rate focused on high-mass galaxies suffices to reproduce the observed shift in mass ratio during cosmic time, and that this rate is consistent with the paradoxical growth of massive galaxies. Therefore, the turn-over in the mass ratio between stars and gas, as well as the paradoxical growth of massive galaxies, can be explained by the same physical mechanism influenced by the rate of bulge construction during the early universe. Sensitive analyses of model parameters reveal that this conclusion holds true, and that the results remain reliable with the current level of observational uncertainties. The underlying physics that accounted for the turn-over in the mass ratio between stars and gas observed in the mass function of galaxies can now be considered established, and its potential implications reach beyond cosmic time evolution, potentially shedding light on the local M*-SFR connection turn-over at high masses, and the varied forms of galaxy bulges observed in different environments. The role of bulge construction in the break observed in the M*-SFR connection at high masses is supported by the findings of an independent analysis of a comprehensive galaxy dataset obtained through the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, which demonstrated a turning point in the mass ratio at $10.6\pm0.5$. The dependence of the mass ratio turn-over on the concentration of galaxies also supports this conclusion, as it is consistent with the prediction that the construction of bulges during the early universe would account for the turn-over in the mass ratio between stars and gas observed in the mass function of galaxies. The distribution of bulge-to-total mass ratios obtained in this study is compared to the distributions observed in other galaxies, which provides a new perspective on well-known galaxy populations such as elliptical galaxies,

This paper delves into the source of low performance in VRD tasks due to excessive false positives, attributing it to overemphasis on the mean average precision metric by current models. We propose a two-part solution to enhance the balance between precision and recall. Firstly, we introduce a relative threshold based on recall distributions to set a more rigorous threshold for considering relationships detected. Secondly, we introduce a mask-based zero-shot attribution technique to visually identify relationship patterns that models are currently capable of learning, informing the selection of more suitable datasets for model fine-tuning. Our proposed method demonstrates consistent performance improvements across two VRD datasets, the Visual Relationship Detection and the Fusion of Visual-Lingual Relationships. We also explore the relationship between model performance and task difficulty through the introduction of a difficulty scoring system, demonstrating that our proposed method delivers consistent performance across various difficulty levels. Our code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/VRDChallenge.

Recently published research indicates that strong solar flares may result in the generation of high-energy neutrons, protons, and electrons through accelerated particles interacting with the sun's atmosphere. As a result of these interactions, neutrons and some types of electrons are capable of penetrating the sun's grasp and reaching the earth. The authors modelled the solar flare that occurred on November 7, 2004, using comprehensive Monte Carlo simulations based on detailed satellite data, and demonstrated that an increasingly intense neutron flux can be generated through the interaction of high-energy protons with the sun's atmosphere. Furthermore, the model predicts that extremely sensitive detectors at low altitudes would be able to detect neutrons that have been converted to light as they interact with the sun's atmosphere, and that the spectral analysis of these interactions would match the spectrum of the solar flare that generated them. The evidence is particularly relevant to the development of accurate neutron detection methods, and the inherent sensitivity of the authors' algorithm means that it could be applied to analyze a wide range of solar flare data. The research was conducted by a team from the University of Degu, with additional contributions from the University of Florence and the University of Toulouse. The authors suggest that it would be beneficial to calibrate neutron detection instruments at the earth's surface by comparing satellite data with the effects of neutrons interacting with the sun's atmosphere. The recently launched Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph spacecraft has the capability to provide more accurate information about solar flare electron spectra, which in turn will enable more precise simulations and a better understanding of the relationships between electrons, neutrons, and protons. The research has significant implications for the development of accurate neutron detection methods, and the team is now working on a more advanced algorithm that will allow for the separation of neutrons and protons based on the characteristics of their interactions with the sun's atmosphere. The authors believe that this technique could be used to detect extremely high-energy neutrons that originate from solar flares, which in turn could provide valuable insights into the extreme magnetic fluctuations that occur at the sun's core. The recently launched Solar Neutron Detector Network consists of multiple detectors located at different altitudes, which can detect high-energy neutrons at a range of heights, and the team is now working on developing a simulation tool that will allow for the simulation of solar flare neutron interactions with the atmosphere based on satellite data, and the detection of neutrons by ground-based detectors. The authors suggest that this tool could be beneficial in predicting the effects of solar flares on the earth's magnetic field

A recent observation of a massive hot dense spin of about 6.5 hours in KIC 9267654, an extremely red giant star, has sparked significant interest. To explain the observed high angular momentum, researchers propose a planetary ingestion event, which would be uncommon, or an unexpected massive angular momentum transfer, which has no known precursor. Alternatively, another possibility exists: a spinning core formed as a result of a supernova, surrounded by dense matter that was formed during the giant phase. If the core is assumed to be entirely composed of iron, with a significant amount of spin energy, not enough angular momentum is generated to account for the observed amount. However, if some of the core is made up of silicon, enough angular momentum is produced, which aligns with the observed value of 6.5 hours. This possibility would be consistent with the giant's surface and spin characteristics, as well as provide insight into the internal dynamics of extremely massive giants. Furthermore, it would make the star susceptible to a Bardeen-Press-Wheeler instability, leading to a spin-induced oscillation in the surface density and potentially causing a planetary ingestion event. Quantum interactions between valleys in silicon's crystal structure are thought to impact the flow of spin information between devices built from this material. Researchers have been able to visualize this phenomenon first hand by scanning atomic arrangements with a precision microscope, and have mapped the patterns of this interaction across individual silicon atoms. They have also determined the degree to which this interaction influences the flow of information and the transfer of spin, and have discovered that higher-energy valleys do not contribute significantly, simplifying the necessary calculations. By utilizing a computational model that mirrors these findings, they have demonstrated reliable performance of silicon-based spin transistor devices. Moreover, this approach has been shown to combine efficiently with silicon's natural encryption method, known as quantum valley isolation, to create perfect channels for spin information between devices built from this material. Lastly, this study has implied that silicon devices have the capacity to utilize the energy stored in atomic vibrations to facilitate smooth transfer of spin information between devices built from this material. Lastly, researchers have been able to utilize this approach to calculate the effects of atomic defects on silicon devices, providing further insights into their functioning.

Complex systems consisting of multiple components, whose interactions shape the overall dynamics, are widespread in scientific fields such as biology, physics, and sociology. These systems often operate under dynamic rules that can switch between modes or exhibit erratic behavior, presenting a significant challenge in capturing their underlying characteristics. To unlock the underlying mechanics of these systems from empirical data, researchers typically rely on reverse engineering approaches that can be computationally expensive and theoretically complex. In this research, we propose a novel framework based on graph neural networks that enables the direct prediction of system dynamics from observed time series data, without requiring inverse modeling. We demonstrate the efficacy of this framework on synthetic datasets and real-world data from physiology, showcasing its ability to accurately forecast state trajectories and recover the system's governing equations. Additionally, we explore the robustness of our method by conducting additional experiments on datasets with limited data, and datasets generated by system dynamics with unknown parameters. These experiments highlight the advantages of our proposed framework in recovering system dynamics and predicting state trajectories even when the system's parameters are unknown. We also analyze the proposed framework's performance in comparison to inverse modeling approaches, and provide a theoretical explanation of its predictive capabilities from a machine learning perspective. The code for this research is available at: https://github.com/ghoul101/Dynamical-Graph-Networks.

A significant challenge in treating stroke lies in identifying appropriate therapies to promote brain recovery and prevent further damage. Advanced treatments such as transcranial magnetic stimulation and cell-based therapies have shown promise but their effectiveness depends on accurate targeting of healthy brain areas around cerebral lesions. Precision targeting requires precise mapping of past lesion locations, which can be achieved by generating a personal brain lesion mask for each individual. Deep learning techniques, particularly variational autoencoders, have been successfully applied in medical imaging but often overlook the important role of data generation and often limit their encoding to small dimensions. A novel approach is proposed here which utilizes a three-part framework consisting of encoder, progressively larger encoders, and discriminator for data generation and validation. Encoders in this framework gradually build up encoded dimensions to generate new samples, which are then passed to a discriminator to validate the generated cerebral lesion masks. This approach is applied to real MRI data featuring cerebral lesions with the goal of generating new individualized brain lesion masks, which can be used for targeting in stroke treatments. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of this approach in accurately representing real data and in combining with registration techniques to create practical targeting protocols. Furthermore, this method demonstrates significant potential in enhancing clinical trials related to stroke treatments. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/ghrasoul/VAE-Cerebral-Lesion-Generation.

To seamlessly transition between these tasks, a modular structure that combines siamese and convolutional neural networks has been proposed, enabling a unified framework for feature learning and selecting the most suitable data set for supervised learning. A subsequent layer matches the distribution of the two data sets, allowing for an index that can be used to determine the level of similarity between them. Experiments conducted on multiple datasets, including MNIST, OIRF, and CASIA, demonstrated a superior performance compared to alternative methods, including the use of benchmark models such as ResNet, VGG16, and MobileNet. Furthermore, the scalability and versatility of this network were highlighted by successfully adapting it to face recognition following a simple modification. The results have been compared to those obtained using state-of-the-art techniques including ArcFace and SoftTriNet, revealing a notable improvement of 2.5% in the accuracy achieved. The source code for this project is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/Abdul88/FaceFingerPrint. Working with nominal data poses unique challenges due to its ordinal nature. Essentially existing in the form of categories or rankings, it doesn't fit well with traditional linear models. While models such as the Group Lasso have been effective for handling high-dimensional data, they struggle with nominal data. To achieve this, we're converting nominal data into integer values, however this results in the Group Lasso's convex optimization problem becoming non-convex. To overcome this difficulty, we propose a new algorithm based on the coordinate descent method, which can efficiently solve this problem by using the Group Lasso's sub-grad. Not only does this algorithm work for hyperplane selection, but it can also be extended to handle soft-group Lasso and Focused Group Lasso. Moreover, this method can be combined with penalty terms and bootstrap sample aggregation to enhance its performance. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we've conducted a range of experiments on realistic data sets. The results show that our method outperforms the conventional Group Lasso and offers greater accuracy in comparison with statistical models such as the multinomial logistic regression and the multinomial mixture model. Recent advances in large language models have achieved high performance on numerous natural language processing tasks, surpassing the capabilities of traditional machine learning methods. Despite this progress, many challenges remain in leveraging these models for real-world applications. One such obstacle is integrating external knowledge to enhance model effectiveness. Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modeling. Subsequent application to Rayleigh-Benard convection yields encouraging results as even a rudimentary model successfully replicates the prevalent characteristic overturning patterns of convection over a wide range of driving forces, accurately estimating the associated heat transfer scaling across six orders of magnitude. Nonetheless, a persistent and considerable error is observed in relation to direct numerical simulation references, underscoring the need for further development, particularly in relation to ascending fluid boundary treatment and the incorporation of additional sub-filter variation modeling. Nonetheless, this paper remains the first known attempt at simulating Rayleigh-Benard convection using a multi-fluid framework, to our knowledge. The approach and obtained research results are also applicable to the simulation of atmospheric convection. The paper at large is an open contribution to the ongoing discussion on the development of multi-fluid models in relation to atmospheric convection. The associated code is publicly accessible as an open source contribution, with the associated results and research approach available for further development and improvement by the scientific community. The associated methodology, successful replication procedure, and code installation instructions are detailed in the Appendix. The framework of the multi-fluid model, its application to Rayleigh-Benard convection, and the associated code are also graphically presented in the accompanying figures. The paper remains an open call for further collaboration with the aim of refining the multi-fluid framework for the simulation of atmospheric convection. A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior. Our analysis indicates that both black hole heat capacity and shadow radius exhibit step functions during phase transition transitions. We also observe the shadow radius to behave smoothly in the phase transition region. Finally, we examine the impact of the non-linear YM charge parameter on shadow radius and the heat capacity jump height, finding that both dimensions decrease as the parameter increases. We discuss our results in the context of the gauge theory side, utilizing the black hole shadow as a probe of the gauge field configuration on the AdS side. We propose that the shadow radius represents the gauge theory's energy density, and that the heat capacity jump height is comparable to the energy difference between the two thermal scalar operators in the gauge theory. We further propose that the sharp transitions in the heat capacity and shadow radius can be the result of multiple trace relations between the vacuum polarization and the gauge field configuration. We conclude that the shadow radius and heat capacity exhibit similar behaviors in the phase transition region, and that both are influenced by the non-linear YM charge parameter. To address this issue, we investigate reinforcement learning with extensive action spaces of various sizes, taking into account the trade-off between diversity and coherence. Our key finding indicates that larger action spaces initially enhance coherence but eventually compromise diversity. To overcome this limitation, we develop a novel threshold-based strategy, restricting selected actions to a minimal set that meet a quality standard, thus maintaining coherence while increasing the chance of discovering high-quality actions, as demonstrated in our experiments. This approach achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods while significantly reducing the difficulty of difficulty exploitation. In the quantum realm, such driving forces result in non-equilibrium steady states governed by unique laws. A recent study accurately describes the behavior of a periodically driven qubit, utilizing either laser radiation or electrical signals, and compares the theoretical predictions with experimental data obtained using a qubit located in a magnetic field created by a microwave resonator with a highly asymmetric shape. The study further highlights the difference between its behavior and that of its equilibrated counterpart in a closed system. We analyzed data from the Inner Magnetosphere Electron Detector Suite on board Parker Solar Probe and found that the solar wind speed has a minimal impact on the energy distribution of electrons within the inner heliosphere. Contrary to expectations, the reduction in solar wind pressure gradient around 20 solar radii did not result in a noticeable increase in electron energy. This lack of effect is thought to be caused by the significant influence of the solar magnetic field and the resulting electron trapping within the solar wind streamers. Instead, we observed a drop in electron energy within the solar wind streamers at radial distances between 20-40 solar radii, which is believed to be a result of electron deceleration due to decreased solar breeze pressure. This deceleration becomes more apparent at greater radial distances and may have implications for the understanding of the solar atmosphere and the behavior of electrons within the inner heliosphere. Further analysis is needed to validate these findings and consider alternative explanations. The data utilization code for these findings can be accessed via the Parker Solar Probe Instrument Data Interface. The observed electron energy decay within the solar wind streamers may be related to the occurrence of recurrent collapse events in the solar atmosphere. The energy distribution of electrons also exhibited a power law in the 20-40 solar radius radius region, which requires additional research to determine its cause. The data analyzed originated from the first four close approaches to the sun, specifically the 4.5, 7.8, 12.2, and 24.6 solar radius radii, and covered a time span of 5.9 days surrounding the closest approach in each instance. The electron energy distribution was found to adhere to the same power law in all of these instances. The use of the Inner Magnetosphere Electron Detector Suite allowed for detailed analysis of the solar breeze effects on electron energy distribution by providing high-resolution data on electron energy and density within the inner heliosphere. A phenomenon of concealed order emerging from random noise has been observed, which allows for the precise measurement of a varying distance in an adhesive tape system. The change in distance is accurately determined by analyzing the time it takes for a crack to occur between the rotation of a pick-up sensor and the application of a force, which remains consistent across different rotation speeds. Consequently, this approach enabled a reliable and precise assessment of surface energy changes during the de-adhesion process. A notable increase in surface energy was observed prior to the initiation of sticking, which precedes the phase of sticking shown in earlier research. Furthermore, two distinct phases of sticking were identified based on the sound patterns, cumulative distance, and surface energy. In this model, individuals are represented by nodes on a network, with higher-connected individuals having greater access to education. The distribution of connections among individuals follows a power law, which leads to a fragmented network structure. To examine how this network affects the distribution of educational outcomes, researchers found that it results in a hypergillyan distribution of outcomes, extreme inequality that affects the majority of individuals harshly. Furthermore, the model highlights that social isolation can sometimes be a survival strategy for those with fewer connections, as it prevents the disappearance of those individual's descendants. Additionally, the model shows that even with perfect meritocracy, the system takes thousands of generations to significantly reduce extreme inequality. A key factor contributing to extreme inequality's persistence is the time it takes for a network's distribution to change. A similar principle applies to other systems that exhibit a slow response to change, such as the distribution of wealth or knowledge. A notable real-world example can be found in the social network represented by a family tree, which shows that the time it takes for a different distribution of children per family to affect the entire generations is also measured in thousands of years. A possible intervention to reduce extreme inequality could be altering the network's structure by targeting the time it takes for a system to change, rather than the system itself. This approach is more feasible than directly altering the system, as it envisions reducing the generations' gap in a matter of centuries rather than thousands of years. A mathematical model can be compared to empirical data represented by a family tree, specifically that of the Indian ruling class, which spans over two millennia. A detailed analysis of this data reveals that it conforms to a logistic distribution, which is a self-similar and fractal distribution that can be found at both a individual and a group level. This perspective on reducing inequality also emphasizes the importance of individual agency, as it is influenced by both genetic and environmental factors, which are represented by the network and its distribution. A mathematical approach is used to examine the interaction between these factors, which provides further insight into the complex relationship between these elements and the time it takes for a system to change. This relationship can be manipulated to optimize the distribution of outcomes, which in a ideal scenario leads to a more uniform distribution. In the 1920s, Kazimierz Menger developed the concept of generalized angle function between subspaces of a vector space, which led to the use of functional inequalities as a basis for metric and angle structures. Two problems that had been puzzling researchers for centuries were then impacted by his work: the first, concerning the convexity of geometric functions, and the second, regarding the additivity of angle functions. Both of these results were achieved through the application of a fundamental inequality called the subadditivity inequality, which also gave rise to a non-trivial generalization of the well-known inequality known as Jensen's inequality. This paper delves into the historical context surrounding these issues, details Menger's contributions, and explains in clear terms the mathematical concepts involved, utilizing Menger's own words and explanations to do so. Furthermore, the paper also examines the various implications of Menger's work, including its impact on the development of abstract metric and angle structures, the use of functional inequalities as their basis, and the resulting generalization of geometric and analytic concepts. Additionally, it explores modern generalizations of Jensen's inequality, analyzes the relationship between absolute norms and metric structures, and examines the connection between angle functions and metric structures, which has been achieved through the use of a concept called the Banach algebra. Lastly, the paper concludes by examining the influence that Menger's work had on notable mathematicians, including John Archibald, Paul Erdos, Gergely T. Rieze, and Albert Wilansky. This paper is intended for readers with an interest in the historical development of mathematics, specifically in the area of geometry, and it is hoped that it will serve as a meaningful contribution to the advancement of their knowledge. The paper is divided into three main parts, each of which is further subdivided into chapters, as follows: part one, comprised of chapters one to three, details the background and historical context surrounding Menger's work; part two, comprised of chapters four to seven, examines Menger's contributions in depth; and part three, comprised of chapters eight to ten, explores the impact and influence of Menger's work. The appendices, which are comprised of chapters eleven to thirteen, provide additional information on the subject matter discussed in the paper. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive analysis of these schemes was previously unfeasible. However,, a high-level observation of the Forsage pyramid scheme became possible by interviewing its practitioners and reviewing related smart contract code. This research reveals Forsage's intricate operating mechanics and identifies key participants such as initial creators, stuck investors, and fraudulent beneficiaries. By examining the condition under which investors fall into any of these categories, a mathematical model is developed that maps the movement of coins to a pattern of paths on a cube. This model enables a thorough understanding of Forsage's dynamics and offers statistical insights into the distribution of coins gained by investors. Furthermore, by utilizing a controller-based representation, it becomes apparent that Forsage's protocol is vulnerable to exploitation through the creation of fake accounts, which could contribute to the scheme's aggressive growth. This representation also facilitates the detection of scams by identifying patterns in the distribution of coins gained by investors. In the case of Forsage, such pattern indicates the presence of altered payment rules that favor a select group of investors at the expense of the majority. This situation is comparable to that found in other general pyramid schemes, yet unlike them, it was discovered through a silent observation of actual transactions among participants. This discovery is significant because it reflects the inherent appeal of these schemes to human nature, as depicted in classic myths such as Orpheus's tragic story. This research was motivated by the widespread popularity of the Forsage scheme, which has been endorsed by well-known public figures and has generated a significant amount of money. This is in addition to the fact that the underlying mechanics of this scheme are reflective of the dynamics that govern relationships and human behavior in general. This knowledge is not limited to the exclusive domain of economics but rather has implications for other fields of study that deal with complex networks and dynamics, such as biology, computing, and sociology. This knowledge is further demonstrated through the development of a simple simulation that showcases the challenging nature of detecting scams, the unpredictable dynamics of coins gained by investors, and the elusive nature of human deception. This research also offers a theoretical explanation for the sudden appearance and disappearance of scams, which is facilitated by a dynamic analysis of the distribution of coins gained by investors. This analysis further reveals the underlying patterns of scams that remain hidden from static observations, as evidenced by the case study of Forsage. This knowledge is critical for developing effective detection methods

The catalog of the Milky Way bulge's globular clusters compiled by Ornitelli et al. (2020) also includes 19 candidates whose status as clusters is uncertain. To evaluate these potential clusters, we investigated their cores using the VVV survey data and found that 13 out of the 19 suspects have core luminosities within the typical range for globular clusters. However, only 7 of these 13 have the bright luminosity typical of cluster cores, which could indicate that the others are subgiant populations. Furthermore, we determined the horizontal branch (HB) luminosities for the 19 candidates, found that the HB luminosities are concentrated in a narrow range around -0.15 magnitudes relative to $\omega$ Centauri, and used this information to classify the candidates as globular clusters with metallicity likely intermediate between [-0.7, 0.0]. Additionally, we compared the candidates to the bulge's horizontal branch stars based on their color and vertical field population, which confirmed that the candidates reside in the bulge and are composed primarily of horizontal branch stars with some giants and a smaller amount of main sequence stars. Moreover, we determined the specific location of the horizontal branch stars relative to the cluster's luminosity, which could be useful for future surveys of the bulge. Lastly, we found that the candidates' distributions are similar to that of the established bulge clusters, which could imply that the bulge's cluster population is uniform. Nonetheless, further research is needed to validate these findings based on other data sets, particularly spectroscopic measurements of their metal content. Additionally, we suggest that the 4 candidates without the typical core luminosity are likely globular clusters with higher metal content, which could include 3 with HB luminosities brighter than typical and 1 with a HB luminosity less bright than typical. These possible higher metal content clusters have HB luminosities similar to those found in the omega Centauri globular cluster and could have a broader range of metal content including masses similar to that of the omega Centauri. Furthermore, we propose that the 4 uncertain candidates be designated as VVV-GC S1 to S4. Lastly, we offer advice for future surveys that will be capable of confirming the status of these candidates through spectroscopic measurements, which will be crucial for better understanding the bulge's cluster population. Deep learning techniques such as Recurrent Neural Networks, Long-Short Term Memory, Gated Recurrent Units, and LSTMs with neural network have gained acceptance in predicting business processes. Although there is growing interest in these methods, little is known about their relative performance in process forecasting. This study examines how different deep learning techniques effect input data, activation functions, and output forecasting and provides a neural network-based comparison to enhance understanding and inform business applications. Our research involves analyzing 12 different techniques including combinations of neural networks with different layers and activating functions to forecast enterprise processes. Our findings reveal that techniques involving a single layer often predict better initial process values while combinations forecast more accurate long-term outcomes. Furthermore, our study discovers that replacement and continuation forecasts can be improved by fine-tuning activation functions and re sequencing input data. Our study includes a supplementary dataset containing 10 additional enterprise processes for future research. By evaluating these results with other evaluation methods such as AIC, BIC, and MAPE, our study provides a deep learning framework to forecast enterprise processes that can be applied to similar research in the field of economics. The massive, explosive event seen from the superflare stellar imitator, AD Leo in near-ultraviolet wavelengths was analyzed through the modeling of its spectrum. This modeling helped separate the signal of the explosion from background stellar spectra and facilitated a detailed study of the event's emission. This research reveals the emission spectrum of the largest known explosion from AD Leo, and it shows that this explosion's near-ultraviolet spectrum is comparable to that of another well-known stellar imitator that experienced a massive explosion in 1994. Although the 1985 explosion from AD Leo was significantly more powerful than the 1994 explosion from another star, its near-ultraviolet spectrum is similar in terms of the spectral features presented. This similarity is interesting because it is typically assumed that the near-ultraviolet spectrum of these types of stars remains constant. This research also explores the possible causes of the 1985 explosion from AD Leo, and it suggests that it could be induced by massive flares that occur as a result of the interaction of white dwarf material with metal-rich accretion spots on the surface of the associated low-mass star. This research was accomplished by combining high-signal-to-noise ratios of the 1985 explosion's spectrum from two separate observations, and it provides a comprehensive understanding of the near-ultraviolet emission spectrum of these types of explosions, in addition to revealing the possible mechanisms that drive them. This research was also accomplished by analyzing pre-and post-explosion observations of AD Leo over the course of two decades. This analysis revealed that the near-ultraviolet emission spectrum of AD Leo either remains constant or only changes slightly over time, and it provided key insights into the possible causes of the 1985 explosion from AD Leo. This research was also accomplished by combining the analysis of pre-and post-explosion observations of AD Leo over the course of two decades with the results of a comprehensive stellar evolution model that tracked the evolution of this low-mass star over the course of its lifetime. This research was also accomplished by analyzing the density and chemical composition of the expanding cloud of gas that resulted from the explosion, and it provided key insights into the possible causes of the 1985 explosion from AD Leo. This research was also accomplished by comparing the density and chemical composition of the expanding cloud of gas that resulted from the explosion with the results of a comprehensive stellar evolution model that tracked the evolution of this low-mass star over the course of its lifetime.
