In this work, we introduce a new clustering method called Influence-Based Graph Clustering (IBGC) specifically designed for dynamical systems modeled on networks. These models comprise nodes representing variables and directed edges representing the causal relationships between these variables. The approach we present focuses on identifying subnetworks where the variables are consistently changed in the same direction throughout time. Unlike existing techniques that rely on fixed rules to determine the orientation of causal relationships, IBGC utilizes data to determine these connections. Furthermore, by converting the problem into a mixed-integer linear programming issue, the method enables seamless integration into existing optimization frameworks for various applications, such as optimization of dynamical systems and robust clustering. We demonstrate the effectiveness of IBGC by applying it to random generated networks and real-world data, showcasing its superiority over alternative methods in preserving the structure of the network and accurately capturing the dynamics of the system. Moreover, we showcase the practical utility of IBGC in a real-world context, such as in the optimization of epidemiological dynamics on complex networks. The code for IBGC is available at https://github.com/amin-ahmadi/IPBC.

Animal population studies often rely on capture-recapture data, where individual animals are identified and tracked within a defined space, providing valuable information about population size and distribution. Additionally, researchers gather data on animal-use patterns from resource selection functions, which detail the preferences of animals for specific habitats, offering insights into behavior, habitat needs, and conservation requirements. This study combines the advantages of capture-recapture and resource selection data by analyzing the spatial patterns of capture locations, enabling accurate population size estimates and informing conservation efforts about population distribution, behavior, and habitat needs. A new model is presented that incorporates capture-recapture data, resource selection functions, and spatial randomness to estimate population size, density, and distribution, and to characterize animal-use patterns. This model excels in areas with dense populations and can also handle multi-season studies, and it serves as a foundation for further development of more complex models that may account for factors like birth and death rates. A software package is available to perform these analyses using the R programming language. This study demonstrates the value of combining capture-recapture and resource selection data, and it offers a versatile tool for biologists, conservationists, and wildlife managers seeking to manage populations and conserve habitats effectively.

The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a higher level of accuracy than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the transmission of solutions within multilayer networks of oscillators by reducing them to a standardized form. This approach enables us to investigate the transmission of solutions by considering the connection between layers, rather than the specifics of the inter-layer connections. By leveraging this method, we are able to determine the conditions under which solutions can be transmitted across layers and the resulting dynamics on a multilayer network. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the reduction to a standardized form provides a meaningful representation of the original network, allowing us to track the dissemination of solutions in multilayer networks. Our study on a representative example demonstrates how our approach can be applied to complex multilayer networks, featuring both identical and heterogeneous component networks. Our general method can be extended to a wide range of network architectures, providing a blueprint for investigating the transmission of solutions in multilayer networks of oscillators. Our analysis has significant implications for the theory of multilayer networks, offering a novel perspective on the transmission of solutions that can be applied to a broad range of networks, as well as a tool for predicting the dynamics of these networks, and can be extended to quantify the impact of changes to the network on the transmission of solutions. Our method has been customized to investigate the transmission of solutions in multilayer networks of stochastic pendulums, as well as to determine the stability of the synchronized state in multilayer networks of Kuramoto oscillators. Our results on the Kuramoto model reveal that the phase response properties of the inter-layer connections are responsible for driving the system out of the synchronized state, whereas the transmission of solutions in this model is governed by the Kuramoto model's natural instability. Our research has also found that the transmission of solutions in the Kuramoto model is insensitive to the strength of the inter-layer connections, as well as the specific phase response properties of these connections. Our analysis has further discovered that the Kuramoto model's natural instability can result in the dissemination of solutions in one component network affecting the other component networks, even at great distance, without the need for direct connections. Detecting and managing traffic congestion rely heavily on estimating traffic flow parameters such as the space mean speed, density, and flow rate. These estimates can be challenging to obtain, especially in areas with limited traffic data. This research presents a novel, nonparametric approach to estimate short-term traffic densities during light to moderate traffic conditions. The method involves analyzing the distances traveled between consecutive detections of the same vehicle and utilizes these distances to estimate density within a 10 to 30 second time frame. This approach has been tested and compared to ground truth data obtained using a mobile radar, with results showing that the estimated densities match the actual densities obtained using the radar. Furthermore, the method has been applied to data from various road types and speeds, and the accuracy of the estimates has been evaluated using radar data as a standard. The findings indicate that the proposed algorithm accurately estimates densities even in the presence of slow-moving traffic and complex road configurations. The method has also been found to outperform traditional space-time estimation techniques in such conditions. The proposed combinatorial method is versatile, nonparametric, and easy to implement, making it suitable for real-world traffic density estimation challenges. The method can be further enhanced by incorporating additional data or signals that provide speed information. The proposed algorithm has been designed to operate autonomously, but it can also be utilized as a component of larger estimation frameworks. The research highlights the potential of probe vehicle density estimation in reducing the costs and challenges associated with deploying mobile radar devices. The findings can be applied to various traffic flow estimation applications, including but not limited to density estimates. The proposed method has been made available to the research community through a public website. The research also emphasizes the significance of combining data from probe vehicles with different detection frequencies. The proposed algorithm has been compared to a standard space-time estimation technique, and the results have been presented in the research. The findings can be improved by analyzing the traffic flow conditions and configuring the algorithm accordingly. The research has been conducted in the United Kingdom, Australia, and New Zealand, and the findings can be applied to these and similar traffic conditions. The proposed method has been designed to operate in the absence of weather or road work information. The research has been funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council. The proposed algorithm has been developed by a single researcher, and the results have been verified by multiple independent parties. The research has been conducted over a 12 month period, and the findings have been presented at an international transportation conference. The proposed method has been developed in conjunction with the University of Southampton.

The Nernst effect, an indirect consequence of the Hall effect, is a promising approach to investigate the topological nature of materials. A recent discovery exemplifies the Nernst effect's uniqueness in kinetics by lacking any assumption of uniform chemical potential, and this phenomenon has selective scattering mechanisms' fingerprints that are all topological in origin. Our study focuses on manganese nitride (Mn$_3$NiN) thin films to explore magnetothermal transportation. Advanced composite materials, incorporating electrically conductive fibers, offer the potential for both structural support and self-diagnostic capabilities. As these materials detect and report damage, their electrical conductivity is altered, providing insight into injury types and extents through changes in their electrical properties. While this feature facilitates maintenance and extends lifespans, the process of damage detection remains challenging due to the presence of uncertainty in input parameters and limited sensory data. To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with the finite element method and electrical impedance tomography to accurately identify and model the distribution of conductive fibers, followed by the determination of injury patterns based on sensed electrical data. The effectiveness of this approach was demonstrated using numerical examples and a test piece made of carbon fiber reinforced polymers, subject to impact testing. The results show that this strategy can determine the location, size, shape, and type of damages, as well as the degree of degeneration, with a high level of precision. Furthermore, the analysis highlights how uncertainty in the distribution of conductive fibers affects the accuracy of damage detection, and the potential for this method to be applied to real-time injury detection through the analysis of temporal changes in electrical properties. The potential improvements to the algorithm, particularly in regards to the resolution of fiber distribution and its impact on damage detection, are also discussed. The potential applications of this technology to other problems, such as the detection of defects in layers and interlaminar damage, were also examined. This article presents an innovative approach to achieving whole number solutions for the diophantine equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$, a more challenging variant of the well-known and historically significant Euler and Pell equations. By applying a change of variables, the equation can be transformed into a form that generates solutions for the original equation. We then establish criteria for these solutions, extending the basic case to higher power solutions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that 7 must be a prime number by analyzing the basic case when the power is fixed, and we derive a relationship with another Diophantine equation, $x^2+xy+y^2=2^m$. Additionally, we explore cases where the power is variable, resulting in the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^m \cdot 9^m$, which can be factored into a product of two Euler equations. We also offer specific examples and a historical context involving the renowned mathematician Albert W. Goodman. This research focuses on advancing the design of a monopod for hopping on soft, uneven ground by conducting numerical analysis and physical experiments to evaluate and improve the robot's design. Initially, a computational model was developed to simulate the interaction between the robot and a soft surface using the finite element method, which was effective in assessing the impact and subsequent hopping phases. However, it failed to accurately replicate the formation of cracks in the ground. To address this limitation, a alternative computational model was developed based on the discrete element method, which provided a more precise representation of the ground surface and the interaction with the robot. This method enabled a deeper understanding of the hollowing effect and the influence of surface hardening around the point of contact. Combining the insights gained from both simulation approaches, improvements were made to the robot design, including increasing the angle of the foot to enhance stability and reducing the impact speed to decrease ground distortion. These modifications led to a successful increase in height achieved during hopping. Furthermore, a novel way was found to calculate the work done on the ground during hopping by integrating the area of the contact patch over time, which can be readily accessible using simulation tools. The increasing complexity of modern information systems necessitates a full-system approach to ensure security and trustworthiness. Achieving this requires analyzing and validating systemic patterns of information, representing relationships between systems, applications, data, and communications. A viable solution demands an effective graph-based methodology that can scale to large networks. This paper introduces an efficient framework utilizing graph algorithms to identify structural elements in information networks. We demonstrate the framework's applicability to a wide range of networks, incorporating popular operating system, software, and hardware components. By leveraging an extensive library of common network elements, it takes just 2 seconds to extract the framework for the Linux network stack. Furthermore, we detail a real-world example involving the Apache Web Server on Linux, showcasing how the framework reveals potentially malicious code structures and identifies vulnerable configuration elements. The framework's scalability is showcased through an evaluation of compilation times for various network configurations. This research has implications for developing reliable, secure information systems and provides a foundation for further advancements in this area. We make the framework's source code publicly available on GitHub. Quantum annealing within a suitable interval can lead to successful outcomes, however, the loss of quantum coherence during deployment can make this suitable interval difficult to establish. Our research demonstrates that by examining the development of quantum coherence during a quench, one can determine the optimal annealing interval, even in the presence of system defects. We tested this approach on a version of the exact cover problem and found that it successfully recovered the quantum annealing success rates reported in previous studies. Furthermore, our analysis exposes the fundamental causes of quantum coherence development, tied to the presence of a particular issue-specific matrix element, and highlights the impact of defector inclusion, thereby providing a clear understanding of the complex dynamics underlying this problem. Our findings also showcase the effectiveness of our approach in recovering successful quantum annealing outcomes by re-executing the simulation with a modified parameter set that ensures defector inclusion, thus offering a way to overcome the obstacle of defectors in quantum annealing deployments. Our research was conducted using a 14-qubit quantum annealer and involved analyzing the dynamics of a single quench scenario, however, our results can be extended to other similar contexts, such as quantum metalearning and quantum reconfiguration, where the annealing interval can be influenced by quench dynamics. Our investigation utilized the exact cover problem as a case study, but the underlying principles are applicable to a broader range of combinatorial optimization problems. Our approach provides a general methodology for enhancing the effectiveness of quantum annealing deployments on various problems by analyzing the dynamics of a single quench scenario. Our research demonstrated that in a particular instance, with a problem size of 24 variables, it was possible to recover the successful quantum annealing outcomes reported in previous studies by re-executing the simulation with a modified parameter set that ensured defector inclusion, however, as the problem size increased to 36 variables, the amount of generated junk matrix elements became unmanageable, resulting in an intractable quantum annealing deployment. Our findings suggested that the optimal solution for such large-scale deployments is instead a classical simulated annealing algorithm due to its superior performance in comparison to quantum annealing in this instance. We investigate a variety of quantum states made from single-photon states, whose phase space is mapped using the quobis representation. Analyzing both squeezed and non-squeezed states, we examine the structure of their phase space to determine the conditions under which they behave as compassionate states. Our research reveals that in certain situations, coherent states and states made from multiple photons also qualify as compassionate states. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases. VSI is influenced by gas properties and can limit the formation and growth of VSI by heating rather than cooling gas. Observations indicate outer solar system protoplanetary disks have dust particles despite expectations they should disappear. A thermal diffusion instability (TDI) may contribute to this presence by distributing particles to deeper layers. However, TDI's impact on VSI is unclear. A recent study investigated the effect of enhanced dust development on VSI in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, specifically focusing on whether it's resistant to VSI or controlled by VSI, or if it's influenced by VSI or stabilized by it. The results show that even in the presence of VSI, dust development can persist in the inner area of the disk and that VSI's impact lessens with distance from the central star. Furthermore, in the middle area of the disk, VSI becomes resistant to dust development, and in the outer area, it breaks down dust development completely. The decay of VSI in the outer area of the disk also becomes slower with increased particle depth. Consequently, enhanced dust development cannot prevent the onset of VSI, but it does influence VSI's behavior, and VSI's impact lessens with increasing distance from the central star. This study's findings suggest that both VSI and TDI need to be considered in modeling dust development in the outer regions of protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick gas cooling. The disappearance of dust in these systems would have far-reaching consequences, leading to larger particle sizes, greater radial instability, and better distribution of silicon particles. The model also indicates that dust development's influence cannot be ignored, and it cannot be scaled down or removed without misrepresenting the systems' characteristics. The presence of TDI is confirmed to be necessary for maintaining silicon particle distribution and preventing their displacement to the inner area of the disk system. The distribution of particles in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick gas cooling makes them resistant to massive migration, thus preventing the formation of too close planetary systems. The model further indicates that both VSI and TDI are stabilized by increasing the temperature of gases or moving further from the central star, which is in line with expectations that higher temperatures and greater distance from the central star would make the systems more resistant to VSI and TDI. Recently introduced dynamic entrance networks have been shown to be effective in addressing classification challenges that involve multiple tasks. By generating task-specific weights for different classes, these networks automatically direct their attention to relevant data. However, a common limitation of these networks is their reliance on classification labels during training, which hinders their use in scenarios requiring label discovery. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel dynamic entrance framework called TIE (Which-I-Should-Evaluate), which produces an internal gateway that connects different data to different outputs based on internal weights, thereby eliminating the need for class labels during training. To demonstrate the versatility of TIE, we employ it in both labeled and unlabeled settings – in the latter case, we pair it with a state-of-the-art density estimation method known as MMD-DN. Our proposed model exceeds existing dynamic entrance methods and matches the performance of fixed networks in experiments involving labeled datasets. Furthermore, TIE exhibits strong performance in scenarios involving label discovery, which involves both low and high-dimensional data. Our recommended approach for training TIE, along with theoretical validation of its underlying properties, is also outlined in the paper. To effectively address open-domain commonsense question answering, it's essential to explore methods that analyze the connection between questions and available web documents. Current approaches primarily focus on incorporating rich representations, without considerable attention to the semantic relationships between questions and selected documents. In this paper, a novel strategy called Coarse-to-Precise (C2P) is presented, featuring a two-stage question answering approach that initially employs a coarse model to generate an initial answer, and then uses this result to guide a precise model using a relevant subset of web documents, based on their similarity to the question. The proposed method is evaluated using the CommonsenseQA dataset and achieves superior performance compared to baseline approaches. Moreover, C2P demonstrates improved results when applied to other open-domain question answering datasets, showcasing the effectiveness of this approach across various tasks. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/zwang95/Coarse-to-Precise.

Quantum systems' behavior can be highly unpredictable due to their intricate interactions, which lead to chaotic developments. Identifying chaos in these systems is crucial, yet it requires precise calculations of entropy across all local sites. To simplify this process, we developed a graph neural network framework that generates an intuitive, scalable representation of entropy distributions, allowing it to effectively detect localized, system-wide chaotic developments by mapping graphs into a single, unified chaos metric. This approach, combined with a new temporal learning protocol, enables precise detection of chaos in finite time periods and accurate classification of dynamic systems based on their chaos levels. Our findings were confirmed through applications to both realistic and simulated models, including a 32-site Hubbard model and a 19-site Shannon map, and demonstrated our framework's potential for generalization across various systems. By harnessing the explainability of graph neural networks and implementing a spatial and temporal attention mechanism, our protocol can be applied to any complex dynamic system for chaos-level assessment. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChaosQuantum/GraphNeuralChaos.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying framework that evaluates these methods remains unclear. Has difficulty in tackling this issue been genuinely reduced over time? To address this question, our pyKT platform is used to establish a clear methodology for benchmark comparison, and reveals that advances in modeling have indeed led to significant improvements in performance. Furthermore, pyKT's feature-rich environment allows for exploration of complex issues, such as variable task definitions and model-based user behavior, which contribute to performance variability. By analyzing user interactions as model-based events, we observe that incorporating temporal interactions reduces performance difference to less than 10%, indicating a limited impact of interactions on task performance. On the other hand, performance disparities of over 50% remain evident across different models, suggesting a need for further development in that area. Our pyKT findings and benchmark framework are now available online at https://pykt.org/.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing their updates can become a major obstacle. The asymptotic optimization performance of leading algorithms under unconstrained gradients is often degraded due to synchronization delays. Existing unconstrained gradient algorithms require devices to wait for previous updates to be confirmed before contributing new updates, limiting the number of devices that can participate. We fill this gap by developing a new algorithm that allows unconstrained gradients and handles delays, and show that it coexists with delayed updates and unconstrained gradients, leading to optimal optimization performance under certain conditions. We also analyze and optimize the performance of this algorithm in various scenarios, showing its superiority over existing methods. In our experiments, this algorithm delivers noticeable performance gains when the number of participating devices is large. In addition, we find that allowing unconstrained gradients during the buffer-filled period does not significantly impact performance, unless the interval between updates is extremely large. In the special case of a single controlling server, our algorithm simplifies to existing leading baselines, showing that it is a unified and generalization of these baselines. In our simulation, we also develop a new version of the algorithm suitable for extremely large datasets, and demonstrate its effectiveness. In this simulation, allowing unconstrained gradients during the buffer-filled period leads to noticeable performance gains. We open-source our code for public use. Our results contribute to the optimal performance achievable under unconstrained gradients and synchronization delays, and our algorithm provides a framework for applying leading baselines from non-federated learning. Our simulation simulates real-world scenarios, and our code is compatible with popular federated learning frameworks. Recently, significant performance gains in speech recognition are achieved by incorporating vast amounts of text-based knowledge from the internet through web-page automatic processing. Nonetheless, numerous challenges arise when attempting to leverage such knowledge, primarily due to the noisy and frequently speech-free nature of web pages. Additionally, online pages are often multilingual, giving rise to further difficulties in developing an effective speech-to-text system. In this research, we present an innovative strategy to overcome these obstacles by exploiting non-speech data within web pages through ASR transfer learning in a "rough-to-fine" approach, initially employing a coarser model to perform initial recognition, and then refining the results with a more precise model. We also explore a cross-language ASR transfer application of our method, demonstrating effective multilingual ASR performance on English and Japanese data. Experimental results reveal our approach yields notable improvements in word error rates (WER) compared to conventional baselines, with the "rough-to-fine" method achieving a 9.4% WER reduction on Google's web pages and the cross-language approach achieving a 12.6% WER reduction on Wikipedia contents. Moreover, our research shows that utilizing web pages with associated labels yields a 5.6% WER reduction when compared to using unannotated web content. Our code is publicly available at GitHub.

Research in navigation systems for marine robots focuses on combining internal sensors with external signals like radio frequency (RF) transmissions to provide precise location and velocity information. Despite the benefits of such combined systems, they can be compromised by jamming or placement difficulties, making RF-based navigation appealing. However, this approach suffers from the drawback of unable to determine the rate at which the navigation signal changes, a critical factor in finding the optimal filtering method. In this study, we address this challenge and develop a novel algorithm to estimate the rate of change in navigation signals based on Gaussian process models, combined with a sparse representation to handle sudden variations in the environment. We also develop a simulation platform for RF navigation in marine environments and demonstrate our algorithm's effectiveness in real-world scenarios. In one real-world test case, our algorithm was applied to data collected from a marine robot operating in Sydney Harbour. Evaluating accretion rates is crucial for understanding the mass evolution of young stars and their surrounding disks. While measuring these rates is straightforward, they can be difficult to accurately determine, especially for stars with unstable or varying mass transfer rates. Our previous research found a short timescale ($\sim$5.75 days) fluctuation in the mass transfer rate of XX Cha, in addition to the well-known long timescale patterns seen in young stars. Observations from the PENELLOPE campaign have now allowed us to further study this star over a longer period, combining its data with previous measurements. Our analysis reveals that the mass transfer rate distribution is bimodal, indicating that XX Cha exhibits two different mass transfer rates that shift over the observed cycle, as well as a gradual long timescale variation. This result challenges current models of disk evolution and mass transfer, and highlights the complex behavior of this system. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the difficulty of measuring accurate mass transfer rates in systems with unstable mass transfer, and stresses the importance of considering multiple viewing angles in the analysis of such systems. We also find that the dispersion in accretion rates observed in young stars may be influenced by the presence of irregular mass transfer, and that a simple correction for this effect could significantly reduce the scatter in their data. Lastly, our analysis provides insights into the dynamics of XX Cha, offering a possible explanation for the fluctuations in its mass transfer rate based on the irregular shape of its disk, as well as revealing that this system exhibits a disk mass similar to that of other young stars. The precise measurement of its mass transfer rate has also allowed us to determine more accurate values for its stellar and disk parameters, including its mass, radius, luminosity, age, mass of its disk, and surface gravity. The extensive data we have collected for XX Cha will continue to be useful for monitoring its behavior, and our analysis provides a framework for understanding the dynamics of this system that can be applied to similar stars. The methods we have developed for measuring mass transfer rates and understanding the dynamics of young stars and their disks should also be applicable to other systems, and the correction we have identified for unstable mass transfer rates could be relevant to other areas of astrophysics that involve the analysis of fluctuating signals. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among agent trajectories. In particular, most current methods fail to adequately utilize positive trajectory data, thereby neglecting a wealth of valuable information. To address this limitation, this paper focuses on finding the most beneficial trajectory data among existing sets and incorporates the most effective data into a batch reinforcement learning approach. By leveraging both high-efficacy individual actions and coordinated interactions, our method achieves superior results in comparison to state-of-the-art baseline techniques across a range of experiments involving multiple interacting agents. Our code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/ChengjunTeng/PPTR.

In large-scale FDD systems, due to limited channel feedback, baseband precoding, and antenna configuration are often shared across many users. To enhance encoding feedback, research has focused on codeword development and evaluation using Gaussian mixture models (GMMs). This paper introduces an efficient method for estimating the quality of GMM-based codewords and proposes a two-step feedback encoding approach. In the first step, users evaluate the codewords using GMMs and feed back the standard deviation and GMM-based quality assessment to the base station. In the second step, the base station rejects unlikely codewords based on the received information, reducing feedback burden. To further increase efficiency, the base station is proposed to update GMMs locally using gradient descent algorithms. In addition to the two-step feedback encoding approach, this paper investigates the use of GMMs to develop codewords for users with difficult-to-estimate channels. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods. This paper discusses GMM-based codebook development and feedback encoding in FDD systems, investigating efficient methods to develop codewords, encode feedback, and baseband precoding. Simulation results validate the proposed approaches and the base station-induced codeword development method. This research can be applied to baseband precoding codebook development and feedback encoding in FDD systems. This paper is suitable for inclusion in the IEEE Communications Letters. To understand the intricate behavior of nonequilibrium surface processes in lattice models, particularly in the 3D Hofstadter model, we have developed a theoretical framework. This framework, based on a rigorous expansion in the tunneling ratio, reveals stable nonequilibrium states characterized by directed surface flows, and demonstrates that these states can be described by a precise statistical measure known as the nonequilibrium density matrix renormalization group (neDMRG). By comparing our theoretical results with neDMRG simulations, we have gained a deeper insight into the dynamics of the 3D Hofstadter model, especially in its fully filled scenario. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the robustness of these nonequilibrium states, showing that they remain stable under local perturbations, and provides a physical explanation for this stability. Additionally, we have investigated two modification scenarios: changing the shape of the lattice and introducing disorder, which also lead to stable nonequilibrium states. Lastly, we have demonstrated that the neDMRG method can be applied to a complex model like the 3D Hofstadter model, and that this method is capable of efficiently describing all its critical features. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 13 actions per second, largely because of strict safety checks required to prevent agents from exploiting exploited exploits.
In response to this challenge, we present TextWorldExpress, a high-performance text-based game that reaches an astonishing one million actions per second, surpassing the previous record by three orders of magnitude.
TextWorldExpress takes the basic structure of TextWorld, yet replaces carefully crafted levels with randomly generated environments, losing the strict safety features that hindered speed in return for unparalleled speed.

Saturn's polar atmosphere changes with the seasons, with persistent polar vortices forming in the winter and disappearing in the summer. During the approach of Saturn's summer, a rare phenomenon was observed in the northern atmosphere - the formation of a polar vortex in the process of developing just above 78 degrees north latitude. It was also noticed that this emerging vortex is contained within a distinct six-sided geometric pattern, a hexagon, and research suggests that this specific pattern may be caused by the balance between an atmospheric instability called baroclinic wave instability and the cooling of the polar region. The formation of the vortex is expected to continue developing over the course of several years, until it reaches its peak in the summer, when it will dissipate. The discovery of the vortex was made using high-resolution images obtained from 2017 and it has been predicted that it will start to weaken in the northern summer of 2026. This finding is significant because it supports the existing theory about the relationship between the size and strength of the polar vortex and baroclinic wave instability, and it also highlights the complex and dynamic nature of Saturn's polar atmosphere. This paper investigates solutions to the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation in a region containing a convex obstacle, and it provides an expansion of the blow-up solutions beyond the previous bound established by Holmer and Roudenko in 2007. Specifically, it shows that the (global) explosion or the breakdown time can be expressed in a particular form, and this expression reveals that the curve defining the phenomenon of explosion has a specific direction near sharp conic ends. Furthermore, in the case of spherically symmetric obstacles, it demonstrates that the solutions that explode must have a particular symmetry and that the curve defining the phenomenon of explosion near a spherical obstacle is a modified version of the Chamberland-Fournier curve, which was originally associated with a different equation. It also demonstrates that solutions that explode cannot occur in the two-dimensional setting. Lastly, it shows that in the case of a regular convex domain with smooth boundaries, there are no solutions that explode. We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero algebraic varieties in a particular type of extension can be precisely determined through a process called local uniform deduction, even when only using the properties of algebraic varieties. This achievement expands on a notable result from a prior study by its primary author, also showing that any local ring that accurately represents such a variety must be essentially of finite type. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a specific class of local rings that are not of finite type are, in fact, generated by a single element, thereby making them equivalent to a specific type of polynomial ring. We also show that in a particular situation, being geometrically integral can be determined by examining the properties of a related subring created through a process called restriction of scalars. This related subring, in turn, contains the prime factors of the original ring and is defined over a specific type of algebraic extension. We also demonstrate that the process of local uniform deduction can be achieved in a semi-parametric form, even when only having access to the elements of the ring $K$ rather than the ring itself. This achievement expands on a prior study by its primary author, also showing that the process of semi-parametric local uniform deduction leads to a ring that is equivalent to the original ring $K$ for the specific case where the ring $K$ is known to be of finite type. We also provide a novel explanation of the process of semi-parametric local uniform deduction for the specific case where the ring $K$ is known to be of finite type, also showing that this process is, in fact, the same as the process of geometric integration over the original ring $K$. We also demonstrate that this process of semi-parametric local uniform deduction can be achieved in a way that is independent of the choice of a specific type of algebraic extension used in the process of restriction of scalars. We provide a series of complicated and technical proofs for these results, also providing a number of difficult examples that are used to illustrate the process of semi-parametric local uniform deduction, as well as the types of rings that are generated through this process. We conclude by demonstrating how the process of semi-parametric local uniform deduction can be used to provide a solution to Hilbert's 10th Problem in the context of a specific type of first-order theory called the theory of polynomials, as well as showing that this process of semi-parametric local uniform deduction is, in fact, equivalent to the process of Tarski's Decision Problem, which is known to be undecidable

The development of experimental tools that can detect and characterize antinucleons is highly challenging but necessary for achieving comprehensive understanding of QCD. While antinucleons are inherently difficult to manipulate and study due to their elusive nature, research suggests they can be utilized as probes within heavy nuclear environments. Specifically, when antinucleons interact with highly dense nuclear matter, they may reveal crucial information about the equation of state, potentially even demonstrating first-order phase transition characteristics. However, extracting this information requires accurate measurement of the energy spectrum of diffractively scattered electrons from the Jefferson Lab's High-Resolution Spectrometer. To enhance the efficiency of this measurement, a new retrieval method for spectroscopic data has been developed, leveraging x-ray diffusion to enhance signal recovery and expanding the range of applicability to include larger scattering angles critical for studying diffractive meson production. Additionally, this approach has been applied to a previous experiment at the Jefferson Lab, yielding a new retrieval technique that can recover complete energy spectra from individual triggers rather than averaged data. Furthermore, this technique has been successfully integrated with simulations, providing a precise and versatile analytical tool for evaluating retrieval performance and signal recovery in experimental scenarios. The development of this method has been made publicly available through a dedicated GitHub repository, demonstrating the feasibility of retrieving antinucleon stage distributions from experimental data and highlighting the potential of this approach for similar scattering experiments in the Jefferson Lab's 12 GeV mode. The effectiveness of this technique has been demonstrated in a specific experimental scenario, involving the scattering of antideutrons off nuclei at an incident energy of 12 GeV, and this method has been found to accurately describe the distribution of signal scatters, thereby providing a precise retrieval technique for spectroscopic data. Hypothesis testing based on Bayesian methods uses Bayes factors, which quantify the ratio of model probabilities with and without the tested hypothesis. Although the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCCM) method is commonly used to compute Bayes factors, its implementation is often challenging due to its high computational requirements and sensitivity to the number of Monte Carlo chains. Alternatively, the bridge sampling method is proposed to determine Bayes factors in a more efficient manner. However, the optimal way to implement this method on a Monte Carlo sample is less clear and needs further investigation. This study examines the accuracy and efficiency of three Monte Carlo workflow strategies for computing Bayes factors using bridge sampling. The results show that two variants of the posterior ratio strategy achieve highly accurate results, with the optimal choice depending on the specificity of the current Monte Carlo sample. Additionally, the study finds that the marginal likelihood strategy is less precise and considers the accuracy of this method's marginal likelihood estimates as critical to its performance. Moreover, the study examines the factors that influence the accuracy of the marginal likelihood estimates and presents a set of best practices for implementing the bridge sampling method, including using multiple Monte Carlo samples and evaluating the accuracy of the marginal likelihood estimates using the Bayes factor uncertainty criterion. This study is applicable to a broad range of statistical models and provides a general framework for evaluating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates based on Monte Carlo samples. This research also addresses the issue of Bayes factor estimate uncertainty in the context of the Bayesian hypothesis testing framework and considers the recent proposal of a new performance criterion that takes into account the uncertainty of the Bayes factor estimates. This criterion is more reliable than the commonly used criterion based on the standard error of the Bayes factor estimates and can be evaluated using the Monte Carlo workflow strategies developed in this study. This research further examines the relationship between the number of Monte Carlo samples and the accuracy of the Bayes factor estimates and finds that the accuracy of the estimates improves at a decreasing rate with the increase in the number of samples. We created a large-scale dataset comprising 6,000 sentences with labeled discourse relationships to train our model, which consists of a discourse classifier and a set of features related to part-of-speech tags, semantic properties, and coherence between sentences. Our research reveals that DiscSense leads to superior performance in ranking the correct sentence for a given context and provides insights into the characteristics of discourse indicators, thereby offering a valuable tool for comprehension model development. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we incorporated DiscSense into a machine reading comprehension protocol involving discourse indicators and discovered that it leads to comprehension performance 10% higher than that achieved when using a random sentence ranking method. A key advancement in 2020 involved developing an efficient and robust tinting method for cubic bipartite graphs on a three-dimensional space. This technique enabled researchers to create graph theories supporting certain divisibility conditions, which in turn led to proofs of several key results in graph theory. A recent study by Ji, Li, and Wang uncovers a counterexample to the divisibility condition required for the edge-colored version of a bipartite graph, known as Chow's Conjecture. Multilingual models are highly effective for natural language processing tasks across multiple languages. These models are based on the concept of a shared semantic space, where words from different languages are represented by vectors that capture their underlying meanings. Despite the success of multilingual models, research continues to explore their fundamental properties. This study examines multilingual shared semantic spaces in English, Spanish, and French, using benchmark datasets for machine translation, part-of-speech tagging, and sentiment analysis. Our analysis reveals that the representation of the same word across different languages varies significantly, which can be quantified as a measure of cluster consistency. To enhance cluster consistency without additional data, we propose a simple yet effective approach that adjusts word representations using a multilingual model's output. Our results show substantial improvements in various multilingual NLP tasks, and our proposed approach facilitates meaningful comparisons of the diversity of word representations in multilingual shared semantic spaces. We also explore cluster consistency as a measurable aspect of multilingual shared semantic spaces and provide a theoretical analysis of its implications. Our proposed approach and analysis tools are applicable to any multilingual task and languages, as demonstrated by additional experiments in English and Portuguese. Our code is available at https://github.com/ygyu1993/ClusterConsistent. This paper presents an examination of mid-rapidity particle production for Xe-Xe collisions at a nucleon-nucleon collision energy of 5.44 TeV, across a wide range of transverse momentum from 0.4 GeV/c to 40 GeV/c, for pions, kaons, proton, and phi mesons. Comparative analysis is performed for different centrality intervals of the collisions, ranging from the most peripheral (60-70% centrality) to the most central (0-5% centrality). Relative production rates are determined for various particles across these centrality ranges, revealing distinct tendencies. In more peripheral collisions, particles of similar mass exhibit similar production patterns, whereas in more central collisions, relative production rates differ significantly, with the phi meson showing a notable decrease in production rate compared to pions, kaons, and protons. This reduction in phi meson rate in central collisions is found to be particularly prominent for transverse momenta exceeding 2 GeV/c. Experimental findings are compared to several theoretical models, including hydrodynamic models that account for partial or full chiral symmetry breaking, and quark recombination models that demonstrate agreement with data. In central collisions, the ratio of phi meson to proton production rates is found to be approximately 0.25, whereas in peripheral collisions this ratio is around 0.5. This distinction in ratios across different centrality ranges is attributed to different initial conditions in the collisions, and is further analyzed using a multiplicity fluctuation approach, revealing that the increase in ratio in peripheral collisions is driven by secondary particle production, while in central collisions it is primarily due to initial state fluctuations. This research adds to the existing understanding of particle production in collisions, and paves the way for further study of heavy-ion collisions. Moreover, Xe-Xe collisions at a nucleon-nucleon collision energy of 5.44 TeV offer a suitable basis for establishing reference data for Pb-Pb collisions at the same energy, accounting for the larger size of Pb nuclei which may influence particle production. Consequently, comprehensive datasets for Xe-Xe collisions will continue to be highly valuable in the future. The findings presented in this paper have been used to establish reference rates for particle production in Pb-Pb collisions, and subsequent papers will focus on more advanced analyses of Xe-Xe collisions. The research was conducted using the ALICE detector at the CERN particle accelerator facility, and involves collaborations with theoretical physicists and researchers using various models to simulate the collisions. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and VIO techniques provide a way to achieve this by learning from sensor data, but they typically struggle with temporary gridlocks and diffuse correspondences. This challenge becomes more significant for low-cost mobile devices with limited computational resources. To address this issue, this paper introduces a novel External Memory Attention VIO (EMA-VIO) technique that incorporates an external memory to store past inertial measurements, enabling the network to focus on more significant correspondence patterns and enhancing the correspondence estimation by taking into account past inertial data and eliminating gridlocks. Leveraging a unified state prediction and correction step, EMA-VIO maintains straightforward implementation and minimal memory usage. Experimentation across various datasets demonstrates the effectiveness of EMA-VIO with respect to state-of-the-art methods, especially in densely crowded environments. Furthermore, by implementing a lightweight network, EMA-VIO achieves real-time performance on low-cost mobile devices. We present a framework comprising two phases for achieving FedSI: the initial selection phase, where entities select data based on their individual preferences, and the fusion phase, where selected data is combined across parties. The results show that the proposed approach leads to improved performance compared to baseline methods in both settings. The proposed framework receives further enhancement through the application of sensitive feature-aware FedSI, which enables controlled integration based on specific sensory inputs, resulting in improved generalization with reduced data requirements. This study focuses on advancing terahertz nanoscopy techniques to directly observe and analyze the local dielectric characteristics of quantum circuit components. A novel approach using a scanning terahertz interferometer reveals the dielectric properties of resonators made of different materials, allowing distinction between them. The findings from this study can be utilized for optimizing quantum circuits and providing precise simulation models critical for controlling and operating quantum systems. In 1974, Gelfand and MacPherson established an algebraic method for calculating Pontrjagin classes for a comprehensive algebraic manifold. This process involves a simple and efficient formula using the coefficients from a specific module associated with the manifold's local ring. Although their innovative approach preceded the development of the Chow group and rational cohomology, their work remains highly relevant and utilized in contemporary research. This article provides an enhanced understanding of their groundbreaking method and includes a new proof of their original formula using the Chow group and its associated ring. Additionally, we examine and expand upon their results by utilizing the properties of the Chow group, specifically the behavior of the natural transformation from Chow groups to cohomology and the module structure of Chow groups. This leads to a more nuanced interpretation of their formula and allows for the calculation of Pontrjagin classes for a specific type of algebraic surface that cannot be analyzed using the original method. We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier approaches, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method.

Furthermore, we have used this method to analyze the effects of injection of injected entropy and angular momentum on the evolution of rotating stars, offering valuable insights into their dynamics. This research has further highlighted the significance of considering the effects of injected particles on the formation of massive stars, and the implications of this for the formation of middle-weight compact binaries.

The advanced vibrational detectors used to detect gravitational waves have an overabundance of data, surpassing the capacity of human analysts to manually review in real-time. To address this challenge, a deep learning network is developed to identify signals from neutron star-binary black hole mergers, even for detectors with high noise levels. The developed model, capable of operating on raw time-domain data, achieves a distinction between gravitational waves and noise of 98.6% accuracy and distinguishes between different merger outcomes with a 97.5% success rate. These results demonstrate that, with appropriate training, deep learning models can effectively analyze detectors' gravitational wave data, even on a large scale. Although this specific model has limited generalizability due to limited training data, it serves as a proof-of-concept that can be improved with more comprehensive training sets. Ultimately, this research contributes a commissioned sub-section of the Inspiral Analysis Package utilized by the LIGO Grid Computing Infrastructure. Moreover, the developed code serves as a starting point for future projects, such as analyzing next-generation detectors. Lastly, this work highlights the importance of incorporating physical properties into deep learning models, which enhances the results in this particular case but could also benefit other applications. Finally, the code developed in this research is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ApoorvaKumarL/DeepNeutronStar.

Social distancing measures implemented during the pandemic varied significantly across the world, leading to distinct impacts on urban interactions. This study analyzes the income effects of these measures on visitors to public places in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, which remained largely unrestricted. A difference-in-hists approach is used to evaluate the change in income distribution among visitors following the pandemic, revealing a shift towards higher income distributions. Furthermore, a comparison is made with pre-pandemic data, showing that the income effects persisted even after social distancing measures were intensified. The study finds that visitors from higher income groups continued to frequent public places at similar levels, whereas those from lower income backgrounds experienced a significant decline in visits. The primary contributors to this decline are found to be increased caution among potential customers and reduced foot traffic due to lowered crowd tolerance. The study concludes that the pandemic's income disparity impact on urban interactions remains evident, with a persistent shift towards more exclusive behavior. The findings are expected to contribute to ongoing discussions of balancing economic activity with public health in the context of urban environments. The study utilizes a novel statistical approach that combines historical data with the regression displacement method to control for time-varying individual characteristics influenced by the pandemic. The Ho Chi Minh City example serves as a microcosm for examining the pandemic's impact on a partially open society, offering policy insights and statistical techniques that can be applied elsewhere. The research highlights the long-term effects of the pandemic on urban interactions, revealing a lasting income disparity that affects public places visited by lower income groups. The study finds that the pandemic's lasting influence on urban interactions remains tied to physical distance requirements, TTP limits, and reduced crowd tolerance. The research identifies reduced crowd tolerance as a key factor in the pandemic's lasting income disparity impact, a variable that can be easily overlooked but is critical for understanding the dynamics of urban interactions during and after the pandemic. The Ho Chi Minh City experience suggests that a return to normalcy may be difficult, with the possibility of a permanent shift towards a more closed economy that exacerbates income disparities in urban interactions. The study's findings on the persistence of the pandemic's income effects highlight the need for temporary and targeted financial support to help small businesses and the low-income population adapt to the changed economic environment. The research provides a framework for analyzing the pandemic's impact on a partially open society, examining the income effects of social distancing measures, and evaluating the shift in income distribution among visitors to public places. A single, unified theory explaining the formation of massive stars is lacking, with different pathways proposed based on whether they form in protostellar disks or through the collapse of dense cores. While the exterior environments of massive star-forming regions are observed to be disrupted, the initial conditions are not well-constrained, despite being crucial for predicting the massive star-forming efficiency and its impact on its surrounding environment. This work examines the formation of massive protostars in massive dense cores by assessing whether they assemble over time or nearly instantly, also searching for core mergers that may have occurred during this process. A systematic analysis of multiple markers, including total integrated mass, surface density, and Thompson flux density, reveals that massive protostars form through the accumulation of multiple components, with some cases showing evidence of core mergers. This is supported by simulations and observations of molecular line widths, also indicating that many massive star-forming cores do not instantly form and instead take several tens of free-fall times to assemble, with some cores breaking apart after the removal of external pressure. Although core mergers may not be common, they do occur among massive star-forming cores, and are more likely to happen in crowded regions formed by multiple star-forming cores. Ultimately, this research supports the notion that massive stars form through the collapse of dense cores that assemble over time, also suggesting that core mergers may occur during this process, with important implications for understanding massive star-forming efficiency and the environment in which they form. This research has been applied to interpret the formation mechanisms of massive stars in the galaxy NGC 6334, a star-forming region located in the Milky Way that is known to contain several massive star-forming cores. To extend the Stokes theorem from $n$-dimensional manifolds to locally convex terrains in $\mathbb{R}^m$, we establish a framework using differential forms and a general notion of integration over terrains. This approach is independent from previous formulations by Weyling, Stokes, and Guggenheim for surface integration. We demonstrate that differential forms can be naturally defined on locally convex terrains using the concept of regular functions. Furthermore, we establish that every differential form on a terrain has an integral, which can be computed using a division of the terrain's simplicial complex. This involves a brief introduction to simplicial complexes in differential geometry. We then generalize the notion of integration to higher-dimensional terrains in $\mathbb{R}^m$ by defining $n$-dimensional differential forms as regular functions that transform comprehensively under the group of permutations in $C_n(\mathbb{R}^m)$, and establish that every $n$-dimensional differential form on an $n$-dimensional terrain has an integral. This leads to a general formulation of the Stokes theorem for locally convex terrains in $\mathbb{R}^m$. We also introduce the concept of oriented terrains and show that the Stokes theorem is compatible with an extension of the notion of oriented manifolds to terrains. In the special case of surface integration, we demonstrate that our formulation is equivalent to the classical version using the scalar field double layer potential. We also analyze the properties of the integral operator, including its linearity, continuity, and the fact that it commutes with the restriction operator. This is further generalized to the case of surface integration on oriented surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^3$. We conclude by examining the relationship between the differential structure of a terrain and the properties of the integral operator, and exploring the possibility of defining differential forms directly using the integration operator. This leads to an alternative, more abstract formulation of the Stokes theorem for locally convex terrains in $\mathbb{R}^m$. We also introduce the concept of the differential structure of a terrain as a vector space composed of the derivatives of regular functions, and explore its properties, including its dimension and the fact that it is independent of the specific choice of simplicial complex. For autonomous navigation, especially in complex and dynamic indoor environments, selecting the optimal level of detail for sonar sensors is a critical decision that significantly impacts system independence, size, and energy consumption. This study investigates a novel approach in which the sonar sensors are avoided in selected layers, and we test and validate a corresponding method called "immediate sonar blending" for use in navigation algorithms. In this approach, regions detected by sonar sensors are combined with motion models, and this combination is fed into the decision-making module of the navigation system. We demonstrate our method on a simulated environment and on a real world scenario with a robot equipped with sonar sensors, and our results show that immediate sonar blending navigation performs well even when sonar sensors are unreliable. Furthermore, we find that this method is suitable for a wide range of applications, including outdoor environments, and it provides a significant benefit in reducing sensor size and increasing system independence. Our code is available online at https://github.com/AhmedNaser/sonar-blending.

This paper introduces an innovative method that leverages deep learning-based language models to tackle the problem. Specifically, it utilizes the profiles of fraudulent news, which are derived from massive text datasets via universal pretraining. To account for the diversity of false news, the approach incorporates a score aggregation method through low-frequency words, which are common in fraudulent articles. The proposed technique achieves superior performance in detecting false news on widely used datasets, exceeding the current state-of-the-art performance. Moreover, it demonstrates versatility by exhibiting high detection rates for previously unidentified false news, which serves as a key contribution. This phenomenon has been successfully modeled using a specific type of stochastic partial differential equation (PDE), and its influence has been examined to better understand the averaging effect it has on generating the mean and standard deviation of field values over specified areas. By conducting a comprehensive analysis of this PDE, researchers have determined the exact coefficients for its diffusion equation, which is a significant breakthrough in itself. Furthermore, a novel integral representation of the PDE has been discovered, and this representation enables the derivation of the relationship between the bending effect and the spatial variability of the random field. This relationship is otherwise difficult to determine from the original PDE. We develop a novel iterative method to solve the $\ell_1$-norm principal component analysis problem, tailored for applications where rotational invariance is desired. Our approach yields a linearly convergent sequence of solutions that is inherently insensitive to rotations. We further establish that this method is applicable to an extended version of the problem, including constraints specified by eigenvalues from multiple datasets. In particular, this leads to an original solution for the multivariate problem, where each dataset is represented by a scatterplot in a separate feature space. Our algorithmic framework also accommodates additional features such as sparse data constraints and regression components. We experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by evaluating various scenarios, including simulation tests, real-world image classification using rotationally invariant principal components, and a face recognition protocol involving separate training and testing datasets. We compare our results against existing state-of-the-art methods and find that our approach achieves comparable or superior performance in all cases examined. Our method is underpinned by easily accessible mathematical theory and can be straightforwardly implemented using commonly available software packages. Our algorithmic framework is available online at https://www.ceng.metu.edu.tr/~emre/Research/RFACS.html. Our results are also analyzed from a numerical optimization perspective, involving applications of the Kurzykowski and the Monschowski theorems, which ensure the convergence of our iterative algorithm. We propose a novel objective function for the rotationally invariant $\ell_1$-norm PCA problem, along with a corresponding iterative reweighting scheme that is analogous to the well-known EM algorithm. Our approach can be viewed as a reweighting iteration that is similar to the EM algorithm, and enables us to tackle a range of related problems, including sparse PCA, robust PCA, and multivariate $\ell_1$-norm PCA. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by experimenting with simulated data, real-world images, and a face recognition protocol involving separate training and testing datasets. Traditionally, annotated data have served as resources for training and evaluating natural language processing models. However, due to the rapidly evolving nature of language, newly emerging entities such as memes, which represent a distinct challenge, may have outdated annotations. In this work, a method is developed to revise the semantic annotations of 2000 questions related to emotions by reducing the modification distance between the original annotations and those assigned by a new set of human judges. This method leverages a pre-trained language model to determine potential annotation errors and correct them. The results indicate that using the original annotations yields relatively high scores when comparing the consistency of human annotations, while the revised annotations demonstrate significantly higher quality, as evidenced by a marked reduction in the distance between the annotations of successive pairs of judges. Furthermore, the improvement in revised annotations is observed across all evaluation metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach in enhancing the accuracy of emotion-related annotated data. Finally, using the revised annotations, we classify the sentiment of the original statements and compare our method to the baseline, observing a minor but consistent improvement in classification accuracy across multiple models. The code and data for this project are available at https://github.com/ghrua/EmotionAnnotationReviser.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar environments, having an effective mapping technique is crucial. In this research, we introduce HiTMap, a novel graph-based representation to determine optimal paths in unknown environments. This model divides a map into overlapping rectangular sections, assigning each a distinct distance value, and prioritizes navigation decisions based on section distances rather than precise positioning. We've developed an implementation of HiTMap, including algorithms for mapping, path planning, and node management, and have tested its performance on simulated maps. Furthermore, we've explored the integration of HiTMap with SLAM in simulated environments, utilizing the Gazebo robot simulator. Our results show that HiTMap yields superior performance in comparison to conventional mapping techniques, while also achieving comparable levels to state-of-the-art methods in certain scenarios. HiTMap source code is available online at https://github.com/ethz-assistant/hitmap.

One of the key constraints on scalar dark matter models arises from the lack of observed gravitational influence on Earth's rotation, specifically related to the phenomenon of differential precession in the Earth-Moon system. To explore a range of these models, researchers are investigating ways to directly measure the Earth's internal magnetic field, a key component in this phenomenon. Our proposal utilizes atomic interferometry in conjunction with a novel approach based on the Meissner effect exhibited by superconducting materials to sensitively gauge the Earth's internal magnetic field in the context of a laboratory experiment. By positioning a superconductor near an atomic interferometer, especially if it incorporates matter waves interacting with a superconducting cavity, allows for the detection of change in the magnetic field through the observation of the Meissner effect's manifestation, which directly correlates with a shift in the atomic spectrum. This effect can be quantitatively assessed to determine the magnitude of the Earth's internal magnetic field, and our proposed method sets a new standard for achievable precision in the field. Specifically, our prediction reveals that with an optimized design utilizing nitrogen atomic interferometry, it is possible to reach a precision of one part in 10 to the power of 4 for the Earth's magnetic field, and even higher with other atomic species. This achievement falls within the parameter range that certain models involving scalar dark matter require, and by analyzing various simulation scenarios, we demonstrate that this level of precision is necessary to constrain a broad category of scalar dark matter scenarios, including those involving complex scalar particles, axion-like particles, and massive scalar gravitons, across a wide range of mass ranges from 10 to the power of -13 to 10 to the power of 1.3 GeV. The achievement of this level of precision through atomic interferometry, combined with the inherent scalability of the designed setup, suggests that this method can be further optimized to reach even higher levels of precision, exceeding the requirements of many other experimental setups that involve matter-wave interferometry, and can be achieved in various laboratory settings, including deep underground locations, or in space-based environments, among others. The proposed design also introduces a novel approach for implementing atomic interferometry within a superconducting cavity, which can be further applied to other research areas and experiments, and sheds light on an unexplored aspect of atomic physics involving complex interactions between matter waves and superconducting materials, specifically related to the phenomenon of non-linear response in the atomic spectrum due to the Meissner effect, which can be driven by varying the intensity of the interferometer

We present DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator tailored for object-oriented programming on GPUs. By introducing a novel "allocation region" concept, DynaSOAr optimizes memory usage and reduces fragmentation. A concurrent approach is taken to allocate memory, both globally and locally, to accommodate various use cases and preferences for multi-threaded applications. To accommodate different data structures and different object sizes, DynaSOAr features both fixed-size and variable-size allocation regions. Furthermore, DynaSOAr includes a fragmentation-minimizing scheme for variable-size regions, a critical feature for long-running programs. To enhance performance, DynaSOAr prioritizes memory accesses that minimize re-allocation, and includes a "allocation hint" system to accelerate the allocation process. The effectiveness of DynaSOAr is demonstrated through a range of benchmarks, including popular open-source codes, which show that DynaSOAr outperforms other GPU memory allocators in terms of performance and reduces memory fragmentation. The source code of DynaSOAr has been submitted to an open-source repository for public use. The results shown here have been obtained using an NVIDIA Ampere GPU, but DynaSOAr is compatible with other GPU models including Tesla, Pascal, and Maxwell. The performance gains and reduced memory fragmentation achieved by DynaSOAr are particularly noticeable in codes that utilize many threads, are computationally intensive, and feature objects of varying sizes. The recommended command-line options for compiling and running the benchmarks are provided in the paper, which includes codes developed using popular programming frameworks such as CUDA, OpenACC, and OpenCL. The results show that DynaSOAr delivers a range of performance improvements over other memory allocators, ranging from 10% to 60% in terms of throughput, and reduces memory fragmentation by as much as 80% in certain cases.
